His wand swept from one attacker to another in rapid succession. The first lost his wand, the second crumpled beneath a Stunning Spell, whilst the third was blasted backwards into two of his companions. Remus ducked beneath a curse aimed at his head, pivoted on his heel and thrust his wand towards the remaining Death Eaters.
"Impedimenta! Stupefy!"
One stumbled as though his feet had become trapped in thick mud, leaving the other exposed to the Stunning Spell that followed.
Several jets of purple light came hurtling towards Remus from his left.
"Protego! Protego! Protego!"
The curses rebounded harmlessly against a succession of shimmering shields. Remus glanced over his shoulder to find Professor Flitwick standing atop a piece of fallen masonry, his diminutive stature doing little to diminish the speed with which he wielded his wand.
"Glacius Maxima!"
A blast of freezing air swept across the courtyard. Ice spread rapidly beneath the feet of the advancing Death Eaters, sending several sprawling whilst others found their boots frozen to the cobblestones. Flitwick scarcely waited to admire his handiwork before turning his wand upon another group of defenders in need of assistance.
"I must admit, Remus, being outnumbered quite so considerably is proving rather inconvenient!" Kingsley remarked, stunning an attacker before moving to stand back to back with Lupin.
"You don't say, Kingsley!"
Remus deflected another curse, whilst Kingsley sent its caster tumbling across the courtyard. As the man struck the ground, his silver mask fell away.
Kingsley frowned.
"Hang on a moment..."
There was something familiar about the man's face. Kingsley was almost certain he had seen him somewhere in the Ministry.
Another masked figure rushed towards him.
"Incarcerous!"
Thick ropes burst from Kingsley's wand, binding the man's arms against his sides and sending him crashing to his knees.
"Depulso!"
With a carefully directed flick of his wand, Kingsley blasted the mask from his face.
He recognised this one, too.
What troubled him more, however, was the peculiar vacancy in the man's eyes. Even whilst struggling against his restraints, the wizard seemed scarcely conscious of what he was doing.
"The Imperius Curse..." Kingsley muttered.
He twisted towards the other defenders.
"EVERYONE, BE CAREFUL! Some of these people aren't Death Eaters at all! They're Ministry employees under the Imperius Curse!"
At that precise moment, McGonagall sent another unfortunate attacker running across the courtyard with their body set ablaze.
"Whilst I appreciate your concern, Mr Shacklebolt," she called, turning her wand upon another approaching figure, "we can scarcely afford to distinguish between those attacking us of their own accord and those doing so against their will!"
A curse narrowly missed her shoulder. McGonagall retaliated with a sharp flick of her wand, hurling a cobblestone on the attacker's head.
"Nor do I intend to burden my students with the responsibility of making such distinctions whilst their own lives are in danger!"
"I'm afraid you're right, Minerva. My apologies."
"I am not suggesting that you abandon your principles, Mr Shacklebolt," McGonagall replied. "Merely that you shall have to work considerably harder than the rest of us if you intend to adhere to them!"
Kingsley permitted himself a small smile.
"I'll bear that in mind."
"LOOK OUT!" Remus bellowed.
An enormous shadow swept over the three of them. A giant had raised its club above the courtyard, bringing it down with enough force to crush them all beneath it.
Kingsley barely had time to lift his wand before something intercepted the weapon.
CRACK!
An entire tree trunk collided with the descending club, stopping it several feet above their heads. Splinters scattered across the courtyard as the two enormous weapons ground against one another.
Behind the tree trunk stood Grawp.
And perched upon his shoulder, clutching a handful of his brother's hair, was Rubeus Hagrid.
"Tha's it, Grawpy!" Hagrid roared. "Give 'im what fer!"
With a tremendous heave, Grawp wrenched the opposing giant's club aside, throwing the creature off balance. He drew back his left fist and drove it squarely into the giant's jaw. The blow sent its head snapping sideways, and the creature staggered backwards before collapsing against a section of the courtyard wall.
Several Death Eaters scrambled out of its path.
"Leave the giants ter us!" Hagrid called down to the others.
Kingsley raised his wand in acknowledgement, whilst Remus gave the half-giant an appreciative nod.
"Right, Grawpy! Over there!"
Hagrid pointed towards another giant advancing through the ranks of Death Eaters, swinging its club indiscriminately at the stone statues defending the castle.
"Chuck me, Grawpy!"
Grawp blinked at his brother.
"Go on, lad! Yeh know what ter do!"
With surprising care, Grawp lifted Hagrid from his shoulder and placed him in the palm of his enormous hand. He drew back his arm and, with a grunt, hurled his brother across the courtyard.
Hagrid sailed over the heads of several astonished Death Eaters.
"THIS ONE'S FER WHAT YEH'VE DONE TER OUR SCHOOL!"
Having reached the height of the opposing giant's head, Hagrid clasped his enormous fists together and brought them crashing down upon its skull.
The giant's knees buckled beneath it. Hagrid clung to its hair as the creature toppled forwards, taking several unfortunate Death Eaters beneath its enormous bulk before striking the ground with a thunderous crash.
Elsewhere in the courtyard, Arthur, Molly, Bill and Fleur fought back to back, holding their ground against the Death Eaters closing in from all directions.
Arthur stunned an approaching wizard just as Molly intercepted a curse aimed at his exposed flank. With a sharp upward sweep of her wand, she sent the attacker hurtling into the air before Arthur blasted him into a nearby pillar.
Beside them, Bill ducked beneath a jet of green light and fired a Blasting Curse at the cobblestones, sending three Death Eaters sprawling amongst the debris. Another emerged through the dust, only for Fleur to step across her husband's path, deflect his curse and strike him squarely in the chest with a Stunning Spell.
"Stay together!" Arthur called.
The four closed ranks as another wave of attackers descended upon them. Whenever one broke away to strike, another covered the opening. Molly intercepted a curse intended for Fleur, whilst Bill disarmed a wizard approaching from his mother's blind spot. Arthur had scarcely finished conjuring a shield around them before Fleur retaliated, unleashing a succession of spells through the gaps between their attackers.
Outnumbered though they were, the four fought with remarkable coordination, scarcely allowing an opportunity for the enemy to come between them.
High above the courtyard, two other members of the Weasley family were proving equally troublesome to Voldemort's forces.
Death Eaters mounted upon broomsticks were closing in upon the towers and battlements, where the students had been raining spells down upon the advancing army. Several broke away from the main formation, raising their wands towards the exposed students.
"Not on our watch, eh, George?"
"Wouldn't dream of it, Fred!"
The Weasley twins reached into their robes and produced several small bags of Peruvian Instant Darkness Powder. Waiting until the approaching Death Eaters were within range, they hurled the bags into the air.
An enormous cloud of impenetrable darkness swallowed the approaching broomsticks. Alarmed cries arose from within as the Death Eaters lost sight of both the castle and one another.
"NOW, EVERYONE!" the twins shouted.
The students leaned over the parapets and unleashed a barrage of spells towards the cloud. Flashes of red light disappeared into the darkness, followed by startled yells as broomsticks and their unfortunate occupants began tumbling towards the grounds below.
On the opposite side of the courtyard, Professor Sprout's assortment of magical plants had brought another advancing contingent to an abrupt halt.
Tentacula vines coiled around the ankles of several Death Eaters, dragging them from their feet, whilst others scrambled away from the snapping jaws of the enormous plants. Every attempt to cut through the writhing vegetation left the attackers exposed to spells launched from the castle above.
"Professor! It's working!" Hannah Abbott exclaimed, watching another Death Eater disappear beneath a mass of tangled vines.
"Splendid, dear! But don't put your wand down just yet!" Professor Sprout called, firing a Stunning Spell at a wizard attempting to sever one of the vines. "We mustn't expect the plants to do all the work for us!"
Hannah raised her wand again, joining the students in another volley of curses.
The enchanted statues also had proved invaluable in holding back the assault. Several stone warriors had taken to hacking at the giants' legs, forcing the enormous creatures to stumble as they struggled to advance. Elsewhere, armoured knights formed protective ranks before the defenders, their shields intercepting Killing Curses that would otherwise have struck the witches and wizards behind them. Whenever the Death Eaters attempted to push through, the statues retaliated with their swords and spears, driving the attackers back or sending them sprawling across the cobblestones.
Howeverz for every handful of attackers the defenders managed to bring down, however, another seemed to emerge from the darkness beyond the castle grounds. The courtyard was becoming increasingly crowded, and the flashes of spells illuminated the faces of friends and foes alike.
Nevertheless, the defenders stood their ground, refusing to yield an inch.
Amidst the chaos, two figures quietly broke away from the advancing Death Eaters. Keeping close to the shattered walls, they used the smoke and confusion of battle to make their way towards a narrow doorway leading into the castle. One briefly stumbled over the rubble, only for the other to catch their arm and guide them onwards.
Neither the defenders nor the attacking Death Eaters appeared to notice them. Within moments, the two figures had slipped through the doorway and disappeared into Hogwarts.
******
"Well, we're here," Ron panted as the four came to a halt before the familiar door of the Room of Requirement.
Harry rested a hand against the wall, allowing himself a moment to catch his breath. "Ginny should still be inside. We'll have to get her out before we can change the layout of the room."
The others nodded, and Harry pushed open the door. To their considerable surprise, however, Ginny was not the only person waiting inside.
"Harry!" Ginny exclaimed, rising from her seat.
"Ronald!"
Almost simultaneously, the tall, bespectacled wizard sitting beside her sprang to his feet. The two hurried towards the group, joined by a brightly haired Tonks, who had been sitting in a nearby armchair. Only an elderly witch at the far end of the room remained where she was, occupied with casting a series of enchantments upon the entrance to the passage leading to Hogsmeade.
"Percy?" Ron stared at his brother in disbelief. "What the bloody hell are you doing here? I thought you'd rather sell us all out to the Ministry!" He turned towards his sister. "Ginny, what's he doing here?"
"Well, you see—"
"Because I've been an utter fool, Ronald!" Percy interrupted. "An idiot! An arrogant, pompous prat! I was a—a—"
Ron raised a hand before Percy could continue his rather extensive list of personal shortcomings.
"All right, Percy. That's enough. I think I get it now."
Percy fell silent, looking apprehensively at his brother.
"Look, I still reckon what you did was rotten, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But now's hardly the time to get all soppy, is it? Besides, you're still my brother."
Ron lowered his hand and gestured towards the door.
"If you're really sorry, there's a way you can prove it. Mum, Dad, Bill, the twins... They're all out there, Percy. They need you." His voice softened. "Help them. Please."
For a moment, Percy looked as though he had considerably more to say. His mouth opened, then closed again, and he gave Ron a grateful smile instead.
"That was rather what I had in mind, little brother. Where might I find them?"
"No idea," Ron admitted with a shrug. "But we're Weasleys, aren't we? We're a loud bunch."
Percy gave a short laugh. "I can't argue with that."
He clasped Ron's shoulder, letting his hand linger there for a moment before turning towards the door. Much as the brothers might have wished to talk things through and make amends, everyone present understood that there was little time for a proper reconciliation.
Ron watched his brother disappear into the corridor and let out a long sigh. How he wished Percy's return to the family could have happened under better circumstances, perhaps over one of their usual family dinners at the Burrow, with everyone gathered around the table, arguing over one another and helping themselves to second servings of his mother's cooking. He dearly missed those evenings. But with a battle raging outside, a hurried reconciliation was the best they could ever hope for.
Hermione seemed to sense what was troubling him. She rested a reassuring hand upon his arm, and when Ron turned towards her, she offered him a small smile, which he managed to return with a peck on her forehead. 
Harry, too, was glad that Percy had finally returned to his family, though he too could not help wishing it had happened on a rather less dreadful occasion.
Tonks, who had been standing beside Ginny throughout the exchange, smiled at the younger Weasley before turning her attention to Harry.
"Harry!" She stepped forwards and threw her arms around him.
"Tonks!" Harry exclaimed, returning the embrace. "What are you doing here?"
"I've come to help Remus. Have you seen him?"
It was only when Tonks drew away that Harry noticed how pale she was. Her hands were trembling slightly, and beneath her familiar smile were traces of exhaustion that no amount of brightly coloured hair could disguise.
"Yes, I've seen Remus, but that's not the point. You've only just given birth, Tonks! You're still weak!" Then another thought occurred to him. "And Teddy... What about your son?"
"He's with Mum, Harry. He's perfectly safe," Tonks replied casually.
"That's not the point, Tonks!" Harry raised his voice.
Tonks blinked at him. She had evidently not expected such a response. "Harry?"
"You can't just leave your son to go off and fight a war! You're his mother, Tonks. He needs you!"
Harry placed both hands upon her shoulders. The thought of little Teddy waiting for parents who might never return was one he could scarcely bear to entertain.
"It's bad enough for me knowing Remus and everyone else are out there. Please, Tonks. Don't do this."
Tonks looked at him for a long moment. The smile had disappeared from her face. Bringing her hands up to his, she gently removed them from her shoulders.
"I'm a mother, Harry, but I'm a wife as well. I can't just sit at home knowing my husband's out there fighting for his life." She paused, her expression softening. "And then there's you. You're family to us, Harry. You know that, don't you? I couldn't leave you behind any more than I could leave Remus."
"But—"
"Perhaps you'll understand someday." Tonks managed a small smile. "Teddy's safe with Mum. It's you and Remus who need me tonight. So let me do this, all right? I'll come back, Harry."
She gave Harry's hand one final squeeze before slipping past him.
"Wait, Tonks!"
Harry made a desperate attempt to catch her wrist, but despite her weakened condition, Tonks proved considerably quicker than he had anticipated. She was already through the doorway before he could stop her.
"TONKS!"
There was no answer.
Harry stood staring at the open door, his outstretched hand gradually falling to his side. A moment later, Draceana's fingers slipped between his own. She said nothing, merely holding his hand as he lowered his head.
From the far end of the room came the sound of stone grinding against stone. The elderly witch had evidently finished whatever she had been doing to the passage. After examining her handiwork one last time, she tucked her wand into her sleeve and approached the group, having overheard the exchange between Harry and Tonks.
"I couldn't help overhearing your conversation, Mr Potter. If it is of any reassurance to you, I shall do what I can to keep that young lady out of harm's way."
Harry looked up. The witch was dressed in emerald-green robes and wore a rather distinctive hat adorned with a stuffed vulture.
"Harry, this is—" Ginny began.
"Neville's grandmother, is it?" Harry asked.
"Ah, you remember me." Augusta Longbottom inclined her head. "A pleasure to see you again, Mr Potter."
"But what are you doing here, Mrs Longbottom? Neville told me he'd made sure you were somewhere safe."
"Oh, that silly boy!" Augusta sighed. "Always so concerned for his grandmother's welfare, yet quite unwilling to accept any assistance from her. He's far too considerate for his own good."
"Sounds like Neville, all right," Ron remarked.
"But Mrs Longbottom, it's terribly dangerous out there," Hermione interjected. "We really ought to get you somewhere safe."
"Nonsense, child! I may be advanced in years, but I assure you that I remain perfectly capable of wielding a wand. I came here to lend what assistance I could to the defence of this school, and that is precisely what I intend to do."
She glanced back towards the passage she had been attending to.
"I have just sealed the passage to Hogsmeade behind me. There shall be no turning back."
"But, Mrs Longbottom, that's—"
"Foolish, Mr Potter?" Mrs Longbottom interrupted.
Harry hesitated.
"Perhaps it seems so to someone of your age," Augusta continued. "But there are few things more worthwhile to those of us who have lived as long as I have than ensuring that the younger generation is afforded the opportunity to do the same. I would much rather spend what strength I have left protecting my grandson than cower somewhere safe whilst he risks his life. I hope you won't attempt to stop me, Mr Potter."
Her gaze settled upon Harry once more.
"Now, have you seen Neville?"
"He's out there, fighting," Harry answered, his voice subdued.
"Excellent." There was unmistakable pride in Mrs Longbottom's voice.
"Then I shall go and assist him. And should I happen upon that young lady, I shall keep an eye on her as well."
With a courteous nod, Augusta drew her wand once more.
"Now, if you will excuse me, Mr Potter."
Harry could think of considerably more reasons why she ought not to go, just as he could have thought of a dozen more to persuade Tonks to return to Teddy. But Augusta's words had made one thing abundantly clear. No matter what he said, neither she nor Tonks would change her mind.
By the time Harry looked up again, Augusta had already left the room, her footsteps growing fainter until they could no longer be distinguished from the distant commotion elsewhere in the castle.
Ginny glanced around the room. The armchairs that had been occupied only minutes earlier now stood empty. In the brief time since Harry and his friends had arrived, Percy, Tonks and Mrs Longbottom had all departed to join the battle.
Another distant explosion rattled the room, drawing everyone's attention towards the ceiling. Harry felt Draceana squeeze his hand, and it suddenly occurred to him how much time they had already spent here.
Ginny appeared to have realised much the same thing.
"Everyone," she began, turning towards the four of them, "was there a reason you lot came back here?"
"Yeah, there was." Harry rubbed the back of his neck. "Thought this would be the easy part, to be honest. But that business earlier with Tonks and Mrs Longbottom's rather thrown me," he admitted.
Draceana gave his hand one last squeeze before addressing Ginny. "We need the room, Weasley. Just not in its present form."
"What do you mean?" Ginny asked.
"We need it to become a place where things can be hidden," Hermione explained. "We believe the last relic we're looking for is somewhere in there. Or rather, somewhere in here."
"So we need you to step outside for a bit, Ginny," Ron added. "The room won't change whilst you're still in it."
Ginny folded her arms. "First you lot insist I stay in here, and now you want me out. Unbelievable!"
"That was between you, Mum and Dad! I had nothing to do with it!" Ron argued.
"You were there, Ronald."
"Well, that's hardly—"
"For heaven's sake, Weasley!" Draceana interrupted. "Are you going to move or not?"
Ginny regarded Draceana for a moment before a mischievous smile appeared upon her face. "I will, on one condition. I want a kiss on the cheek from Harry."
"What?" Draceana's eyes widened. "Have you gone completely mental, Weasley? How dare you ask my boyfriend for such a thing when I haven't even—"
"Oh, you haven't?" Ginny's smile widened. "Poor little Malfoy."
Draceana turned scarlet, a rather catlike hiss escaping through her clenched teeth as she glared at Ginny.
"All right, that's enough, both of you!" Harry hastily stepped between them, his own cheeks growing considerably warmer. "Fine, I'll do it if I have to. Will that do, Ginny?"
"Oh, Harry, I'm only joking!" Ginny laughed. "I know how important this is to you."
She glanced at Draceana, looking particularly pleased with herself.
"And that, Malfoy, is how you get him to stop worrying for a moment. You ought to take notes."
"All right. That's it. I'm going to curse you, Weasley!" Draceana reached for her wand, prompting Harry to once again position himself between the two girls. Despite himself, he was beginning to smile.
"I think Ginny and Malfoy are even worse than Malfoy and me," Hermione whispered to Ron.
"Couldn't agree more. Just don't let either of them hear you say that."
"Agreed."

text:
her enormous body coiled within a shimmering sphere of protective enchantments, its faint outline gradually fading into the darkness as the three disappeared from sight.
******
"INCOMING!" Remus Lupin shouted.
An enormous green light swept across the courtyard, casting the shadows of the defenders against the castle walls. Kingsley barely had time to shield his eyes before a deafening explosion sounded overhead. The ground lurched beneath them, rattling the windows of the surrounding towers, whilst loose roof tiles came crashing down into the courtyard.
From their positions high above, several students peered cautiously over the parapets, their wands still clutched in their hands. Professor Flitwick, who had been tirelessly reinforcing the enchantments throughout the bombardment, staggered backwards as his wand arm was thrown aside.
An uneasy silence followed the explosion. One by one, the defenders emerged from behind the stone pillars and archways where they had taken cover, and as McGonagall raised her head, she was relieved to find the protective dome still standing above them. Several others breathed audible sighs of relief, though their reprieve lasted scarcely a few seconds before a sharp crack broke the silence.
McGonagall watched as a fracture appeared across the dome, branching into dozens more until the entire enchantment gave way, shattering into countless luminous fragments.
Oh, dear...
"HERE THEY COME!" Kingsley's voice rang across the courtyard.
Beyond the remnants of the barrier, hundreds of silhouettes emerged from the darkness. At the forefront of the advancing army, Death Eaters and Snatchers rushed towards the wooden bridge, followed closely by several giants whose enormous strides allowed them to keep pace with the considerably smaller figures.
"MR FINNIGAN, IF YOU PLEASE!" McGonagall called towards the tower overlooking the bridge.
High above the courtyard, Seamus Finnigan exchanged a gleeful look with Tracey Davis. Between them lay a circular pattern of runes they had etched into the stone, magically linked to the Blasting Charms they had placed along the bridge's supports.
"With pleasure, Professor!"
The two brought the tips of their wands down upon the centre of the circle, sending a pulse of light through the interconnected runes.
For a fleeting moment, nothing happened. Then, just as the first ranks of Voldemort's army reached the middle of the bridge, an explosion tore through its wooden supports. One after another, the remaining supports erupted in flames, sending entire sections of the bridge tumbling into the ravine. Those unfortunate enough to have made it halfway across plunged into the darkness below, their screams drowned out by the thunderous collapse of the structure.
"BOOM!" Seamus and Tracey exclaimed in unison, grinning at one another.
Their success, however, did little to deter the rest of the advancing army. Several Death Eaters mounted their broomsticks and swept across the ravine, whilst those remaining on foot began shouting instructions to the giants. To Remus's astonishment, one of the larger giants lowered itself across the narrowest part of the ravine, gripping the opposite ledge with both hands and allowing the Death Eaters to scramble across its back.
"Well, that's rather inventive of them," Remus muttered, raising his wand. Much as he hated to admit it, their enemies had adapted remarkably quickly.
"BATTLE POSITIONS!" Kingsley shouted, stepping forwards as the other members of the Order rallied around him. "We hold this ground for as long as we can! Take down as many of them as possible, and don't let them reach the castle!"
As the first wave of Death Eaters descended upon the courtyard, the enchanted statues stepped forwards, raising their swords and shields in unison. Behind them, Kingsley and his fellow mages aimed their wands at the approaching figures.
"ATTACK!!!"
******
Harry had lost count of how many times he had paced the length of the corridor. Draceana was leaning against the wall with her arms folded, tapping her foot impatiently against the stone floor, whilst Ron had taken to sitting cross-legged on the ground, with Hermione beside him, resting her head against his shoulder.
"Where are they?" Harry muttered, glancing towards the wall through which Nick had disappeared. His patience was wearing thinner by the minute.
"Should we go and look for them?" Hermione suggested, lifting her head.
"And have them go looking for us when they've found something?" Draceana pointed out.
"Well... I suppose you've got a point," Hermione admitted.
Harry had just turned to make another journey down the corridor when the entire castle lurched violently beneath their feet.
This was nothing like the bombardment they had endured earlier. Rather than a succession of distant impacts, the tremor seemed to come from one enormous blow, so powerful that, for one dreadful moment, Harry could have sworn the castle had tilted to one side.
"Draceana!"
Harry seized her by the shoulders and pulled her against him, shielding her with his body as she clutched the front of his shirt. Beside them, Ron hastily pulled Hermione into his arms.
Then came a deafening explosion from the opposite side of the castle. The sound reverberated through the corridors, rattling the windows in their frames and sending loose fragments of plaster raining down upon them.
"What the bloody hell was that?" Harry asked, looking frantically about the corridor.
"Harry, look! Up there!" Hermione exclaimed.
Following her outstretched finger, Harry looked through one of the high, arched windows. Against the night sky, the enormous dome of light surrounding Hogwarts was beginning to crack. Fractures raced across its surface until, with a loud crash, the entire barrier shattered, its luminous fragments dissolving into wisps of light.
"The barrier..." Ron gasped. "It's gone!"
Harry stared in disbelief. Barely half an hour had passed since the assault began. Every professor at Hogwarts, together with members of the Order, had contributed to those protective enchantments. Surely their combined magic ought to have held considerably longer than that?
Then it dawned on him. There was one item that might explain how the barrier had fallen so swiftly. Harry recalled the vision he had had shortly before leaving Shell Cottage. He remembered Voldemort hovering above Dumbledore's tomb, his long, thin fingers closing around its handle. And then came the memory of that first, dreadful act. With the item newly in his possession, Voldemort had destroyed Dumbledore's tomb until nothing remained.
"The Elder Wand," Harry murmured.
"What?" Ron turned towards him.
"It must've been the Elder Wand. Voldemort's done this himself."
"Bloody hell, Harry!" Ron stared at the now unprotected sky. "Can that wand really do all that? How are we supposed to beat him?" His conviction wavered slightly.
Harry had no answer. Even if they succeeded in destroying every last one of Voldemort's Horcruxes, they would still have to contend with one of the most powerful wizards alive, now in possession of a wand capable of undoing the combined efforts of some of the finest witches and wizards Harry knew. For a brief moment, Harry found himself wondering whether he had been right to pursue the Horcruxes rather than the Hallows.
"What's an Elder Wand?"
Harry turned towards Draceana, who had only just released her grip on his shirt. He exchanged a glance with Ron and Hermione before remembering that she had not been with them when Xenophilius Lovegood had told them the tale of the Deathly Hallows.
"Really old wand, supposedly made by Death himself. Most powerful wand in existence. Unbeatable in a duel, and so on." Ron explained hurriedly.
Draceana blinked at him. "What?"
"Pretty much what he said," Harry replied. "Though he's left quite a bit out."
"What the boys are trying to say, Malfoy, is that we haven't really got time to explain the whole story. Just believe us when we say it's not a good thing if Voldemort is in its possession." Hermione interjected.
Draceana glanced towards the window. "Fair point Granger."
"Good heavens! What on earth was that dreadful explosion?"
All four turned as Nearly Headless Nick emerged through the wall beside them, looking thoroughly alarmed.
"Nick!" Harry exclaimed, momentarily forgetting the destroyed barrier. "Did you find her?"
"Well, not us, exactly," came Myrtle's voice as she floated through the wall beside him. "But the Bloody Baron did."
"Oh, that's the best thing I've heard all day!" Ron exclaimed, scrambling to his feet.
"Take us, quick," Harry said at once.
"Certainly, my dear boy! Follow me!"
Nick promptly turned and glided through the wall he had just emerged from.
"Sir Nicholas!" Hermione called. "We can't walk through walls!"
Nick's head reappeared through the stonework. "Ah! Of course. My apologies." Emerging once more, he gestured towards a staircase at the far end of the corridor. "This way, then!"
With Myrtle floating alongside Nick, the four broke into a run, their footsteps echoing through the stairwell as the first distant cries of battle reached them from outside.
They hurried along several corridors and up successive flights of stairs before eventually reaching the fourth floor.
"This way, Harry! We're nearly there!" Nick called, drifting ahead of them.
As they pressed onwards, Harry began to recognise some of the portraits hanging along the corridor. There was something oddly familiar about the route Nick was taking them, though he could not immediately recall why. It was not until they rounded another corner that they caught sight of a gaunt, silver figure floating beside a classroom door, his robes stained with patches of silvery blood.
"There he is! The Baron's found her!" Myrtle exclaimed. "She's in there!"
The four skidded to a halt before the Bloody Baron, who acknowledged their arrival with a solemn nod before extending a transparent hand towards the door. Harry seized the handle and threw it open.
Beyond it lay a disused classroom. Several desks had been pushed against the walls, and a thick layer of dust covered what little furniture remained. Whilst Ron, Hermione and Draceana scarcely spared the room a glance, Harry could not quite shake the peculiar sensation that he had been there before.
But standing in the middle of the classroom, her long hair falling almost to her waist, was the very person they had spent the better part of the evening trying to find.
The Grey Lady.
"Oh, thank goodness," Hermione breathed.
Ron bent forwards, resting his hands upon his knees, whilst Draceana released a long breath beside Harry. After so many disappointments that evening, they had finally found her.
The Grey Lady turned towards the newcomers. Her eyes lingered for a moment somewhere behind Harry, and she let out a weary sigh.
"You always did know where to find me."
Harry glanced at his friends. Ron raised his eyebrows, Draceana frowned, and Hermione looked equally puzzled. None of them could make much sense of the remark, though Harry was hardly in the mood for another riddle.
"You're the Grey Lady, aren't you?" Harry asked, approaching her cautiously.
"That is the name by which I am known here, yes."
"And I sincerely hope you don't intend to vanish on us," Draceana added, still rather short of breath. "Neither the occasion nor the state of my legs lends itself to another tiresome game of cat and mouse."
"You needn't worry. I have given my word to him that I shall remain here," the Grey Lady answered.
Harry wondered briefly to whom she had given her word. "Then you know why we're here?"
The Grey Lady inclined her head.
"Then please, you've got to tell us," Harry added.
For a moment, she studied Harry's face. "Will you be like him, I wonder? That boy to whom I once entrusted my story."
Harry opened his mouth to ask whom she meant, but surprisingly, this time, there was little need. He already knew whom she meant. "Tom Riddle?"
She nodded.
"Is that why you've been hiding?" Harry asked.
"I was ashamed," she admitted, lowering her gaze. "And perhaps afraid. How could I have known that the boy to whom I confided my secrets would become what he is today?"
"Riddle was good at getting people to trust him," Harry said. "You weren't the only one he fooled. It wasn't your fault."
"But it was my mother's diadem."
"Your mother?" Ron repeated.
"Oh, for heaven's sake!" Draceana exclaimed, throwing up her hands. "There are people out there risking their lives against that bald freak as we speak. Would you please spare us the cryptic remarks and tell us everything you know?"
"Malfoy!" Hermione reproached her.
"What? We've precious little time as it is, Granger!"
Before Hermione could respond, the Bloody Baron drifted past them and came to stand beside the Grey Lady. To the astonishment of all four, he reached for her hand, enclosing it within his own before giving her a gentle nod.
"But what if I am mistaken again?" the Grey Lady whispered, looking up at him. "I have made one mistake after another. What if this, too, should prove to be another?"
The Baron did not utter a word. He merely tightened his hold upon her hand and nodded once more.
For several seconds, the four watched the exchange in bewilderment. Never before had they seen the Bloody Baron exhibit anything resembling tenderness towards another being, living or otherwise.
"You are right," the Grey Lady murmured at last. "As you so often were."
She turned towards Harry and his friends, drawing herself up once more.
"Forgive me. He can be rather persuasive when he wishes to be. I shall tell you everything."
Harry breathed a sigh of relief. Beside him, even Draceana appeared to have recovered some of her patience.
And so the Grey Lady began her tale.
Her true name, as the four soon learnt, was Helena Ravenclaw, the daughter of Rowena Ravenclaw herself. In her youth, Helena had longed to possess the extraordinary wisdom for which her mother was renowned. Believing that her mother's diadem would grant its wearer unparalleled wisdom, she had succumbed to temptation and stolen it.
Rowena, however, had known what her daughter had done. Rather than confront Helena or expose her theft to the other founders, she had worn a replica of the diadem, concealing her daughter's wrongdoing from everyone. Her mother's kindness had only served to deepen Helena's guilt. Eventually, unable to bear the shame of what she had done, Helena fled to Albania, taking the diadem with her.
As her mother's health deteriorated, Rowena entrusted someone with the task of finding her daughter and bringing her home. It was none other than the Bloody Baron, who, much to the astonishment of the four, had been Helena's lover.
By the time he found her in the forests of Albania, Helena had already concealed the diadem within the hollow trunk of a tree. The Baron had pleaded with her to return, but Helena, still unable to bring herself to face her mother, had refused. An argument ensued between the two lovers, and in a moment of anger, the Baron struck her down.
Helena paused here, her gaze wandering towards the silvery bloodstains upon the Baron's robes. Unable to live with what he had done to the woman he loved, the Baron had taken his own life then and there. He had remained silent ever since, even in death.
By the time Helena finished recounting the Baron's death, none of the four seemed particularly inclined to interrupt her. Hermione had pressed a hand against her mouth, her gaze drifting between the two ghosts, whilst Ron stood beside her with his arms hanging loosely at his sides.
Harry, meanwhile, found himself looking at the Bloody Baron with considerably different eyes. He had passed the bloodstained ghost countless times over the years, never once imagining the tragedy behind those silvery stains.
Beside Harry, Draceana had gone unusually quiet. She was staring at Helena, her lips pressed together, her fingers curled tightly around the fabric of her shirt. There was something disturbingly familiar about parts of Helena's story, particularly the pride and misunderstandings that had driven two people who loved each other towards such a terrible end. Draceana glanced at Harry, and for one fleeting moment, she could not help wondering whether, in another life, the two of them might have suffered a similar fate.
Harry noticed her silence and had a fair idea what had brought it on, though he said nothing. Instead, when he felt Draceana's hand searching for his, he slipped his fingers between hers and gave them a gentle squeeze before returning his attention to the Grey Lady.
At last, Helena came to the part of her story for which they had sought her out.
Many centuries after her death, she had encountered a remarkably charming young student by the name of Tom Riddle. Through his attentiveness and carefully chosen words, Riddle had earned her confidence and persuaded her to reveal where she had concealed her mother's diadem. Helena had never imagined that the seemingly pleasant young man would one day become Lord Voldemort. As the prospect of war drew nearer, the guilt of having entrusted him with her secret had become increasingly unbearable, until she could no longer bring herself to face even her fellow ghosts.
"Hang on," Ron interrupted. "Do you know where the diadem is now?"
Helena shook her head.
"I am afraid not. I thought you wished to know who had taken it."
"That's not—" Harry caught himself before he could finish.
He had scarcely believed how close they had come, only to find themselves at another dead end. Helena's story had confirmed their suspicions that Voldemort had obtained the diadem, but they had already suspected as much. What they needed was its present whereabouts.
Ron let out a groan, whilst Draceana lowered her head, rubbing her forehead with her free hand. Whatever sympathy they had felt for the two ghosts was quickly extinguished.
"Could you at least tell us what it looks like?" Hermione asked, glancing at her disappointed companions.
"It was a silver tiara, bearing the likeness of a ravenclaw insignia upon its crest and adorned with numerous blue gemstones," Helena explained. "I am sorry that I cannot help you with its present whereabouts."
"No, that's quite all right. Thank you, Helena." Hermione offered her a kind smile before turning towards her friends, only to find something rather peculiar.
Harry and Draceana were staring at one another, their eyes wide, the disappointment that had weighed upon their faces moments earlier suddenly gone.
Something about Helena's description had evidently struck them both at precisely the same moment.
"It’s that thing!" Harry and Draceana exclaimed simultaneously. "I can't believe it!"
Once again, they had spoken in perfect unison. Ron and Hermione glanced between the two, looking thoroughly bewildered.
"Ron, Hermione, come on!" Harry exclaimed, already making for the door. "I know where that bloody Horcrux is!"
"What?" Ron stared at Hermione, who looked every bit as confused as he was.
"Just follow you two! We know exactly where it is!" Draceana called over her shoulder as she hurried after Harry.
Hermione opened her mouth, evidently intending to demand an explanation, but the sound of their retreating footsteps persuaded her to wait a moment.
"Just go, Ron!" she sighed, seizing him by the wrist.
“Alright, alright” Ron said as he was pulled out of the room. 
Without so much as an explanation to the bewildered ghosts, the four dashed out of the classroom, once again finding themselves racing through the corridors of Hogwarts.
"Where are we going, Harry?" Ron called breathlessly as they hurtled down the very staircase they had climbed only minutes earlier. "Will you at least tell us?"
"Room of Requirement!"
Harry could scarcely suppress the grin spreading across his face. After hours of running about the castle, chasing one dead end after another, he finally knew where the Horcrux was.
"Why the Room of Requirement?" Hermione called from behind him.
"I've seen it!" Harry and Draceana answered simultaneously.
They exchanged a brief glance as they rounded another corner.
"Go on, Potter," Draceana said.
"Ladies first."
"Isn't it customary for a gentleman to take the lead?"
"You only call me a gentleman when it suits you, Malfoy."
"I do no such thing!"
"Oi, lovebirds!" Hermione shouted, struggling to keep pace with them. "Explain, now!"
A faint blush crept across both their faces. Harry cleared his throat before turning his attention back to the corridor ahead.
"Right! Remember in sixth year, that Potions book I had? The one that belonged to the Half-Blood Prince?"
"How could we forget?" Ron panted.
"Well, when I needed somewhere to hide it, I went to the Room of Requirement. I asked for a place to hide things, and the room changed, just like it did for us in fifth year."
Harry leapt over the last two steps of the staircase, nearly losing his footing before carrying on.
"There were mountains of rubbish in there, but I remember seeing a tiara resting on a box on top of a desk. Silver, blue jewels, everything Helena described! I just didn't think much of it at the time."
"Neither did I," Draceana added, brushing a strand of hair from her face as she ran. "I saw the very same thing whilst I was repairing the Vanishing Cabinet in sixth year. Although, if memory serves, I tossed it aside."
"You did WHAT?" Harry turned towards her in disbelief.
"Oh, don't give me that look, Potter! It was old, dusty and positively filthy. How was I supposed to know it wasn't some ridiculous trinket belonging to a student with exceptionally poor taste?"
Harry groaned. Of all the things she could have tossed aside, it had to be the legendary diadem of Rowena Ravenclaw.
"Well, let's just hope it's still there when we get the room to change!" Harry said as another explosion outside shook the castle. 
******
Meanwhile, in the courtyard below, a silver tabby cat darted between the legs of the duelling witches and wizards. A curse struck the cobblestones where its paws had landed only a moment earlier, but the cat had already swerved aside, slipping beneath another jet of light before narrowly avoiding the enormous foot of a giant.
Spotting a mound of fallen masonry ahead, the cat bounded up the rubble and sprang into the air. Its silhouette lengthened, its paws gave way to hands and feet, and by the time Professor McGonagall emerged from the transformation, her wand was already pointed towards a group of advancing Death Eaters.
"Incendio Maxima!"
A torrent of flames erupted from her wand. Several Death Eaters barely had time to raise their own before the fire swept over them, scattering those fortunate enough to stand away from its reach. McGonagall landed upon the cobblestones, her emerald robes billowing behind her as she turned to meet her next attacker.
Not far from her, Remus Lupin found himself confronted by half a dozen opponents.
"Expelliarmus! Stupefy! Repulso!"

text:
The Walk That Shook the Middle East

On November 19, 1977, Egyptian President Anwar Sadat stepped off a plane in Israel. 

He was the first Arab head of state to visit since Israel's founding in 1948.

 Egypt and Israel had fought four wars, and Sadat's own army had attacked Israeli positions in 1973. Now he was arriving as a guest.  

Why would a leader take that risk? And what did he hope to achieve?

A line that wasn't in the script

The surprise began ten days earlier. On November 9, Sadat set aside his prepared text before Egypt's People's Assembly and said he was ready to travel to the ends of the earth for peace, even to the Knesset itself. 

A U.S.embassy cable sent the next day read the offer as a way of dramatizing how far he would go, not as a serious possibility.
 
The diplomats were wrong.  
On November 20, Sadat addressed Israel's parliament. 

The core of his message was "peace with justice," built on principles that included an end to the occupation of territories Israel captured in 1967. He also demanded recognition of Palestinian rights. 

Begin replied that everything relating to the dispute was open to negotiation. Warm words on both sides did not close the gap between their positions.  

The long road to a treaty
The visit did not solve the conflict. Talks stalled and needed American mediation. Sadat, Begin and U.S. President Jimmy Carter met at Camp David in September 1978. The result was a framework for peace in the Middle East. Egypt and Israel signed their peace treaty on March 26, 1979. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize.  

The price
Most of the Arab world did not follow him. Within weeks, leaders of Libya, Algeria, Syria, South Yemen, Iraq and the PLO met in Tripoli to answer his move. 
The summit declared a "freeze" in diplomatic ties with Egypt. After the treaty, the pressure grew. Arab leaders met in Baghdad and decided to expel Egypt from the Arab League. The League's headquarters left Cairo for Tunis.  

On October 6, 1981, Islamist militants assassinated Sadat during a military parade in Cairo.

Courage or division?

Sadat's supporters argue that he did what no leader before him dared. He broke a cycle of war and recovered Egyptian territory through diplomacy. His critics argue that he made a separate deal, left the Palestinian question unresolved, and cut Egypt off from the Arab world it had long led. Both sides point to real events.

So was Sadat a courageous leader who dared to imagine peace, or a politician whose decision divided the people he represented?

That's the conversation this story deserves.

BY @RDiavolos 
Defenders and Attackers - A Malfoid AU Fanfic
(Writer’s note: this scene takes place during the start of the Battle of Hogwarts.)

Night had fallen over Hogwarts.
Ordinarily, the arrival of night brought a familiar tranquillity to the ancient castle. The last students would be making their way back to their common rooms, the portraits would be settling into their frames, and the corridors would gradually fall silent beneath the watchful eyes of the professors. Beyond the windows, the Black Lake would reflect the stars, while the Forbidden Forest stood dark and undisturbed against the distant hills.
Tonight, however, there was no such peace.
Footsteps thundered through the corridors as students hurried past professors shouting instructions, while the portraits called anxiously to one another for news of what was happening. On the seventh floor, the last of the evacuating students were filing into the Room of Requirement. Several of the younger ones clutched their belongings, reluctant to let go of the hands of their older schoolmates, whilst Professor Slughorn did his utmost to maintain an orderly queue towards the passage leading to the Hog's Head.
Professor McGonagall, having made her way from the headmaster's office, arrived just as Slughorn ushered the remaining students into the passage.
"That should be the last of them, Minerva," he announced, dabbing his forehead with a handkerchief.
"Very good, Horace. I'm counting on you."
"Are you quite sure you wouldn't rather have me here?" Slughorn asked, tucking the handkerchief into his waistcoat pocket. "I dare say I could be of some assistance with the defences."
"I understand your concern Horace, but you also have an equally important task of seeing those children to safety," McGonagall replied. "We are their teachers. Therefore, their safety must come before anything else."
Slughorn glanced towards the passage and gave a reluctant nod. "Very well, then. However, I promise I'll return as soon as I've seen them safely on their way." He drew his wand and straightened his waistcoat. "Godspeed, Minerva."
"And to you, Horace."
Slughorn had scarcely disappeared into the passage when an all too familiar voice came bellowing from within it.
"Minerva! MINERVA!"
McGonagall recognised the voice at once. She drew a small breath and turned towards the passage just as Aberforth Dumbledore came marching out of it.
"Yes, Aberforth?"
"WHY IN THE BLOODY HELL IS MY PUB FULL OF SCHOOLCHILDREN?" Aberforth thought he had asked calmly, when in reality he was shouting.
"They're evacuating, Aberforth. What else would they be doing there?" McGonagall adjusted her spectacles. "Your establishment just happened to be at the other end of the only passage available to us."
"Oh, bollocks Minerva!"
"Whether you believe me or not hardly changes where the passage leads."
Aberforth grumbled something under his breath. For a moment, neither seemed particularly inclined to continue the conversation. McGonagall, however, noticed that one side of Aberforth's collar had folded inwards and instinctively reached to straighten it, only to stop when his eyes followed her hand. She quickly busied herself with smoothing a perfectly presentable sleeve, pretending nothing had happened, while Aberforth took rather longer than necessary to put his collar right.
"Will you be joining us?" McGonagall asked at last.
Aberforth gave a derisive snort. "In your dreams, woman."
"Albus would have—"
"I'm not my brother, Minerva." The change in his voice made her look up. "Never have been, never will be. I've done more than enough for his precious plans. I've fed those runts, kept them out of the Carrows' hands, and now I've got half the school in my pub. Don't ask any more of me."
McGonagall lowered her hand from her robes. "I rather suspected you might say that."
"Then why bother asking?"
"I'm not entirely sure," she admitted. "Hope, perhaps."
"Childish notion. Act your age, Minerva."
McGonagall pursed her lips, deciding that there was little point in trying to persuade him further. However, as Aberforth began to turn away, she remembered the little box she had opened in the headmaster's office. Whatever differences he might have had with his brother, surely he deserved to know about it.
"Aberforth, there's something you ought to know. Albus, he—"
"No, Minerva. I've heard enough about Albus to last me a lifetime." With that, Aberforth made for the passage, though just as McGonagall thought he would leave without another word, he stopped and glanced back at her over his shoulder. "Just try to stay alive, you old hag."
He disappeared into the tunnel before she could offer a reply, leaving McGonagall staring after him with the faintest hint of a smile.
"Still as stubborn as ever," she murmured.
Much as she would have liked to finish what she had been trying to tell him, there was still a castle to defend. Drawing her wand, McGonagall turned and strode out of the Room of Requirement.
******
By the time McGonagall reached the courtyard, the preparations elsewhere in the castle were well underway. Professors, members of the Order of the Phoenix and students who had elected to remain hurried between the towers and battlements, carrying supplies and exchanging instructions as they passed one another. Those proficient in protective enchantments had gathered along the battlements, their incantations carrying across the grounds.
"Protego Maxima!" High above the courtyard, Professor Flitwick raised his wand towards the night sky, sending a brilliant stream of magic over the castle. As the enchantment spread from one tower to the next, its pale light washed over the ancient stonework, drawing the attention of several students who stopped to watch.
"Fianto Duri!" called Molly Weasley from a neighbouring battlement, adding her own enchantment to Flitwick's.
"Repello Inimicum!" Kingsley Shacklebolt followed, prompting several members of the Order to raise their wands in turn. With each successive spell, the barrier extended further across the grounds until Hogwarts stood beneath an enormous, translucent dome.
Whilst her colleagues attended to the protective enchantments, McGonagall glanced along the rows of stone statues lining the courtyard before raising her wand.
"Piertotum Locomotor!"
At once, the statues began to stir. Much to the astonishment of the students nearby, armoured knights stepped down from their pedestals, stone warriors lifted their weapons, and figures that had stood motionless for centuries turned towards McGonagall, awaiting her orders.
"Take your positions along the entrances and battlements," she instructed. "Guard every passage into the castle. Not a single Death Eater is to set foot inside Hogwarts without a fight!"
The courtyard trembled beneath the weight of the marching statues as they dispersed to their respective positions. McGonagall stood aside to let them pass, watching as the very same statues she had walked past countless times throughout her teaching career now marched to defend the school. Her fingers tightened around her wand.
"Come along, everyone! Quickly now, we haven't got all night!"
Just as the last of McGonagall's statues marched out of the courtyard, Professor Sprout emerged from one of the covered passageways, leading a procession of students carrying an assortment of particularly unpleasant-looking plants.
Those nearest the professor were struggling with enormous pots of Venomous Tentacula, ducking and twisting out of the way whenever their thorn-covered tendrils lashed out. The students following them carried wooden crates filled with Chinese Chomping Cabbages, some of which had already begun gnawing through the wood. Bringing up the rear were several students entrusted with pots of Mandrakes, their roots kept firmly buried beneath the soil.
"Finally, we're taking the fight to them, Professor!" exclaimed Neville Longbottom, hurrying alongside Sprout with a particularly troublesome Tentacula in his arms. After months of enduring the Carrows' cruelty, he could scarcely suppress his grin at the prospect of giving the Death Eaters a taste of their own medicine.
Sprout turned towards him, her usually cheerful face growing grave. "Mr Longbottom, I would advise you not to sound quite so enthusiastic. This isn't one of your schoolyard duels. Those people aren't coming here to award points for a well-performed spell."
Neville's grin faltered. "Sorry, Professor. I didn't mean—"
"I know what you meant, dear. However, I must remind you, a war is not a place to get big headed. Lives are at stake here, dear." Sprout interrupted, her expression softening as she noticed a tendril creeping towards his sleeve. "And I'd be grateful if you kept that thing pointed away from your classmates. We should like to have everyone in one piece when the fighting starts."
"U-Understood professor." Neville hastily adjusted his grip, earning a nervous laugh from Hannah Abbott, who had wisely moved a little farther away from him.
"Professor, are we really going to use all of these?" Hannah asked, looking back at the procession of students.
"Every last one of them," Sprout replied, gesturing towards the outer walls, where several students were already unloading their pots. "The Death Eaters may have their curses, but they aren't the only ones who know how to make things unpleasant. A few well-placed Tentacula should give them something to think about, and I rather doubt they'll enjoy having Mandrakes dropped among them." She paused to survey the preparations. "Let's just hope they'll be enough to make a difference."
With that, Sprout ushered her students onwards, calling out instructions as they carried the plants to their intended positions.
McGonagall watched Professor Sprout and her students disappear up the staircase before turning her attention back to the courtyard. Ordinarily, the sight of so many of her pupils working together to defend their school would have filled her with pride. Yet tonight, as she watched them prepare for the coming battle, she found herself questioning whether she had done the right thing in allowing them to stay.
"Minerva."
It was Molly Weasley, who had just returned from the battlements with her wand still in hand. She came to stand beside McGonagall, gazing up at the protective enchantments shimmering overhead.
"Do you honestly think it'll be enough?" Molly asked. "The enchantments, the statues, all those plants of Pomona's... Will they keep them out?"
"Unless you've thought of some extraordinary enchantment that Filius and I have overlooked, Molly, I'm afraid we've done all we can."
Molly shook her head. "No, nothing of the sort."
"Then we shall have to make the best of what we have," McGonagall replied.
Molly's attention wandered towards the staircase through which Neville and the others had disappeared. "I still don't like it, Minerva."
"And what is it that you don't like?" McGonagall asked, though she knew perfectly well what Molly meant. She had simply been reluctant to broach the subject herself.
"These children being here!" Molly gestured towards the battlements, where several students were assisting members of the Order. "Look at them! They ought to be worrying about their N.E.W.T.s, having fun with their friends, making plans for what they'll do when they leave Hogwarts, Minerva. They shouldn't be preparing to fight a war!"
"Molly, those who have remained are of age. We have made it perfectly clear that anyone who wishes to leave may—"
"Oh, for heaven's sake, Minerva! You know perfectly well that's not what I mean!"
McGonagall fell silent.
"I know they've chosen to stay, and I know they're brave," Molly continued, watching another group of students hurry across the courtyard. "But being brave won't stop a Death Eater from flinging curses at them, will it? We both know what those people out there are capable of. And Harry... Oh, that poor boy." She tightened her grip on her wand. "Every year, it's something else. Every year, that boy comes up against You-Know-Who, and here we are, hoping he'll do it again. He's only seventeen, Minerva. Seventeen!"
McGonagall could hardly dismiss Molly's concerns, not when she had seen for herself what the last war had done to so many of her former pupils. There had scarcely been a week in those dreadful years when news of another disappearance or murder had not reached Hogwarts. And Molly, who had lost both her brothers to Voldemort's followers, now had her children somewhere within the castle, preparing to face those very same people.
Before McGonagall could find an answer, the approaching sound of hurried footsteps drew their attention towards one of the passageways.
"Professor McGonagall! Professor!"
Seamus Finnigan came hurrying into the courtyard, accompanied by Tracey Davis and several other students, who seemed to be having a rather spirited discussion about Blasting Charms. McGonagall straightened at the sight of them.
"Yes, Mr Finnigan? What is it?"
"Professor, is it true? About the bridge, I mean." Seamus could barely contain his excitement. "We're really allowed to blow it up?"
"Yes, Mr Finnigan. You have my full permission."
Seamus exchanged an enthusiastic glance with Tracey before turning back towards McGonagall, apparently wishing to make absolutely certain he had understood her.
"Boom?"
McGonagall regarded him over the rims of her spectacles.
"Boom, Mr Finnigan."
"Brilliant! You heard her, everyone! Come on!"
With Tracey and the others close behind him, Seamus dashed off towards the bridge, already discussing where best to place their enchantments. McGonagall allowed herself a small smile as she watched them go. After seven years of teaching Mr Finnigan, she had finally found an occasion on which his particular talent with explosives might prove useful.
Molly, however, could not bring herself to share in McGonagall's amusement. As she watched the students disappear, laughing and arguing amongst themselves over the best way to blow up the bridge, she shook her head and turned towards McGonagall once more.
"We're the adults, Minerva," she murmured, gesturing towards the passageway through which the students had just disappeared. "We're supposed to be the ones protecting them. They shouldn't have to fight our battles."
"Do you imagine I haven't thought of that, Molly?"
Something in McGonagall's voice made Molly turn towards her.
"I have spent years teaching these children, watching them grow up in this very castle. Do you honestly think I take any pleasure in sending them out there, knowing that some of them may not live to see tomorrow?" McGonagall's voice faltered ever so slightly. "If I could send every last one of them home, Harry included, I would. Believe me, Molly, I would."
"Minerva, I didn't mean—"
"Then we must see to it that they don't fight our battles."
Both women turned to find Kingsley Shacklebolt approaching from the staircase leading down from the battlements.
"Kingsley?" McGonagall asked.
"Forgive me, Minerva, Molly. I couldn't help overhearing." Kingsley came to stand beside them, lowering his wand. "I'm inclined to agree with Molly. It was our generation that failed to put an end to Voldemort, and it hardly seems right that we should now be asking children who have barely come of age to fight alongside us."
Molly lowered her gaze towards the grounds. Much as she agreed with Kingsley, there was still the question of whether they had the means to fulfil such a responsibility.
"How many are we expecting to face, Kingsley?"
"At least four hundred, according to our scouts. Possibly more," Kingsley answered. "Death Eaters, giants, Dementors, Acromantulas and goodness knows what else. Altogether, they outnumber us by roughly three to one."
"Good heavens," McGonagall murmured.
"Precisely why Remus and I have given some thought to how we ought to position ourselves. With what little time we have left, we believe the best course of action is for the Order, the professors and the other adult volunteers to meet Voldemort's forces on the grounds, whilst the students support us from the towers and battlements." He gestured towards the castle walls. "They'll have the advantage of height and, more importantly, something solid between themselves and the Death Eaters."
"Even with the assistance of the statues, Kingsley, I fear we shall be spreading ourselves dreadfully thin," McGonagall remarked, surveying the grounds. "One breach in our formation and we risk being overwhelmed."
"I'm well aware of that, Minerva. But I'd sooner have the adults bear the brunt of their attack than risk exposing those children to it."
Neither woman could find anything to say to that. Kingsley turned towards Molly, whose eyes were still fixed upon the grounds.
"I cannot promise you that every child in this castle will come through tonight unharmed. But I give you my word, so long as there is breath in my body, I shall do everything in my power to see that those Death Eaters never get near them."
Molly swallowed, turning her gaze towards the castle. "This war... None of this is right."
"No," Kingsley agreed. "It never was."
Beyond the protective enchantments, the distant hills had all but disappeared into the darkness. Somewhere out there, Voldemort's army was gathering, and all three knew that when midnight came, it would be their responsibility to hold the march back.
******
Meanwhile, somewhere within the castle, Harry Potter and his friends were still searching.
"Mate! Mate! MATE!" Ron called breathlessly from behind the others.
Harry, Hermione and Draceana skidded to a halt just as they were about to round another corner. Having spent the better part of their search running up and down staircases and through seemingly endless corridors, all four were beginning to feel the strain.
"What, Ron?" Harry asked, turning towards him.
"Mate, where are we going?" Ron managed between breaths, bending forwards with his hands resting on his knees.
Harry opened his mouth to answer, only to realise that he hadn't the faintest idea. He glanced towards Hermione and Draceana, hoping that either of them might have something to offer, but both girls merely shrugged.
"Not sure, to be honest."
"What?" Ron straightened, still breathing heavily. "You mean we've been running all this time for nothing? Blimey, mate, this is unbelievable! We need a plan! A lead! Something!"
"I know, Ron, but what?" Harry retorted, throwing up his hands. "We haven't got anything, Ron! Nothing!"
"All right, that's enough, you two!" Hermione stepped between them before Ron could respond. "This is hardly the time for petty squabbles."
"I can't believe I'm saying this, but Granger's right," Draceana remarked, brushing a few loose strands of hair from her face. "I'd rather we go over what we know. We must've missed something."

"I'm right, am I?" Hermione asked, turning towards her with a particularly wide grin.
"Oh, shut it, Granger," Draceana replied with a frown.
Harry and Ron exchanged looks before breaking into amused smiles.
"Well, if those two can play nicely..." Ron said, nudging Harry with his elbow.
"Yeah," Harry chuckled, though his smile faded as he glanced through one of the corridor windows. Beyond the glass, he could see the protective enchantments stretching across the night sky. Everyone outside were preparing for the assault, yet here he was, running around the castle without even knowing what he was looking for.
"Right, then," Hermione began, giving everyone a moment to catch their breath. "Harry knows there's a Horcrux somewhere in Hogwarts."
"And we originally thought it was Ravenclaw's diadem," Draceana added. "Or rather, we still do."
"But nobody's seen the bloody thing in centuries," Ron reminded them, leaning against the wall. "So what are we supposed to be looking for? Anything that looks remotely valuable?"
"I still reckon the diadem's our best lead," Harry said. He began pacing the corridor as he considered what Dumbledore had taught him about Voldemort. "Knowing him, I can't imagine he'd pass up something that belonged to one of the founders."
"Yeah, but there must be thousands of other valuable things in this castle, mate, can't he, I don't know, choose another?" Ron pointed out.
"But how many of them would be as valuable to Voldemort as Ravenclaw's diadem?"
Hermione watched Harry pace for a moment before something occurred to her.
"Harry, what about your connection with Voldemort?"
Harry stopped and turned towards her.
"If he can use it to get inside your head, perhaps you could use it to get inside his," Hermione continued. "You might be able to find out what the Horcrux actually is, or at the very least, where he's hidden it."
Harry considered the suggestion. Until now, he had largely regarded his connection with Voldemort as something beyond his control, something he had been taught to shut out rather than use. Yet if Voldemort could take advantage of that connection whenever it suited him, what was stopping Harry from doing precisely the same thing?
"Good idea, Hermione. Let me try."
Draceana moved a little closer as Harry closed his eyes, trying to shut out the sounds of hurried footsteps and voices coming from elsewhere in the castle. He concentrated on Voldemort, hoping to catch even the briefest glimpse of whatever occupied his mind.
He had scarcely begun when something enormous came hurtling through the window beside them.
Harry felt someone seize his sleeve and yank him sideways as the window shattered, sending fragments of glass flying across the corridor. Whatever had come through it struck the opposite wall with a tremendous bang, showering the four of them with loose plaster and momentarily obscuring the corridor in a cloud of dust.
"Bloody hell! What was that?" Ron spluttered, waving a hand in front of his face.
"Are we under attack already?" Draceana asked between coughs, releasing Harry's sleeve to draw her wand.
Before any of them could make out what had crashed through the window, a remarkably familiar voice rose from somewhere within the dust.
"Sorry 'bout the window, lads! Grawpy got a bit excited!"
Harry lowered his wand.
"Hagrid!"
As the dust began to settle, the enormous figure of Rubeus Hagrid emerged from the wreckage, shaking bits of plaster out of his shaggy hair and beard. Apparently none the worse for having been thrown through a window, the half-giant beamed down at the four students.
"Harry! What're yeh doin' here? Ron! Hermione! And..."
Hagrid's eyes wandered towards the blonde girl standing beside Harry, and his expression changed considerably.
"Miss Malfoy?"
"She's with us, Hagrid. Don't worry," Harry assured him.
"And I've reached the point where I'm quite accustomed to people questioning why I'm in the company of these three fools," Draceana added, with a resigned sigh.
"Well, I ain't exactly surprised," Hagrid replied, scratching his beard.
"You're not?" Ron asked.
"Then what's with the look of disbelief?" Hermione added, looking rather puzzled.
"Well, I jus' didn't reckon Harry'd manage ter win the young miss over quite so soon, that's all. I had a bet it'd happen after all this business was over." Hagrid glanced down at the enormous boarhound emerging from behind his legs. "Didn't I, Fang, old boy?"
Fang gave an enthusiastic bark.
"Fang!" Draceana squealed, immediately crouching down and flinging her arms around the delighted boarhound. Within seconds, Fang was covering her face in slobbery kisses, much to the bewilderment of Ron and Hermione, who were still coming to terms with how dramatically her voice had changed and of course her love for animals.

The General’s Dispatch — Thursday, November 19, 2026

Commanders: The morning’s victory parade ended with the band fleeing alongside the infantry. Preliminary closing figures put the $SPX down 2.03% at 7,175.24, the $IXIC down 2.23% at 23,885.88, and the $DJI down 2.20% at 49,095.46—a surrender of roughly 1,103 Dow points. Anthropic’s grand arrival could not rescue the broader army. 

Anthropic, trading as $ANT, opened shortly before noon at $111.50 after Wednesday night’s $83 IPO pricing, but its initial surge faded. Elsewhere, $AMD tumbled following Hunterbrook’s disclosed short position, $NVDA recorded a sixth consecutive decline, and $CRWV suffered steep losses. $WMT slipped after its annual sales outlook disappointed, while $PANW advanced after raising its revenue forecast. The cybersecurity regiment at least remembered to secure its perimeter. 

Across the intermarket battlefield, the formations disagreed:

• Treasuries: The 10-year yield eased to around 5.05% from 5.07% Wednesday, with demand for safety and softer economic reports supporting bonds. The defensive trenches attracted recruits.

• Gold: December futures settled 1.5% lower at $3,685.50 an ounce, while bullion touched a 14-month low. The imperial treasure chest offered little shelter. 

• Market breadth: More than 90% of S&P 500 constituents fell. This was a retreat across the ranks, extending the index’s losing streak to six sessions—its longest since 2024. 

• Dollar: Dollar strength continued to pressure gold as traders anticipated a December Fed rate increase. The greenback retained its commanding position without requiring a victory in equities. 

The General’s assessment: My reading is that enthusiasm for one celebrated newcomer failed to restore confidence across the market. Broad selling, modest Treasury support, and further weakness in gold suggest investors remained selective about shelter and reluctant to embrace risk.
