Downstairs in the bar, Nicolai-Archie had remained stoic, glittering in his red, black and diamond suit, whilst glaring at the treacherous Charmaine as she pretended to go about her business trying desperately to hide her guilt-laden terror.

As Chester stared into Allyra’s eyes, Archie approached the barmaid with a deliberately slow pace. The men at the bar quickly vacated their seats and took up occupancy in the available booths. Archie sat in front of Charmaine causing her to drop the glass in her hand. The sound of it shattering silenced the lounge.

Chester’s irises circled and waved. Red swirls danced about the deep auburn-browns. They called to Allyra, whispering her name. Her own eyes glowed with an auburn hue,
‘Yes Master?’ She whispered.

Archie caught Charmaine’s fearful stare. The monocle dropped from his eye and bounced on its chain. His lips parted baring smiling teeth, but his eyes sneered,
‘You have betrayed me, Charmaine,’ he snarled, then three voices vomited from his lips, ‘you have betrayed us.’
Charmaine backed away quaking,
‘No, no I haven’t. I promise.’

Chester took Allyra’s chin gently in the palm of his hand,
‘You have no meeting with Charmaine today, do you understand?’
Allyra nodded,
‘Yes Master.’

Archie’s eyes turned grey, and Charmaine stopped trembling, her eyelids grew heavy. She stopped moving and remained still under Archie’s control. Archie twisted his head around to measure the size of the audience who were pretending to see nothing, his neck did not follow.

He pulled his right glove off and blew some dust that had settled into the palm of his hand across the room, then replaced the glove. Everyone except Charmaine and Archie stopped moving and sat temporarily frozen in time. Some grinned, some slumped in their seats open mouthed caught mid-sentence and others stared down at their table avoiding Archie’s gaze. All were motionless.

Chester lifted Allyra, pulled back the blankets, and tucked her lovingly into the bed,
‘Charmaine said nothing to alarm you. DID SHE?’
‘Charmaine said nothing to alarm me, Master.’
He licked her face with his black tongue then whispered,
‘You are mine.’
‘I am yours.’
Chester nodded,
‘Who am I, Lyra?’

Archie hauled himself off the chair and marched to the end of the bar, lifting the enclosing panel, and stood firmly between the optic shelf and the door to the wine cellar,
‘Come, Charmaine, I have someone who wants to meet you.’
‘Yes Sir,’ Charmaine nodded, and followed him through the door and down the wooden steps into the darkness of the cellar.

‘You are Chester,’ Allyra replied. Chester nodded,
‘And who is Chester, my sweet?’

In the cellar a small oil lamp glistened on the wooden stepped ladder used to reach the higher bottles. Beyond the lamp, perfectly silhouetted in the dim light stood a gurney. Leather straps hung either side. A small medical trolley rolled from the darkness stopping at the righthand side of the gurney. The medical trolley housed saws, scalpels, and some unpleasantly thick sutures that glittered with a cruel mirth in the darkness,
‘Lay on the gurney!’ Archie ordered.
‘As you command, sir,’ Charmaine replied. Her body drifted helplessly to the gurney; she climbed on top and lay supine. Archie strapped her in slowly, pulling each buckle tighter than necessary. He completed his duties by taking a small knife from his pocket and dipping it into her stomach, then licking the blade. Archie nodded, congratulating the victim on her flavour, then whispered into the darkness,
‘You can come out now.’

Allyra’s eyes whitened, then reddened, then whitened again,
‘Chester is my man.’
‘Is Chester a man, Lyra?’ Chester laughed mockingly.
‘No Master.’
Chester grunted,
‘Who is Chester?’
‘Chester is a demonic entity. A powerful being.’
‘You must love Chester very much…’
Allyra’s eyes half-closed,
‘Yes Master, you have instructed me so.’
Chester’s lower lip dropped and his eyes saddened,
‘Do you love me of your own accord Lyra?’
Allyra did not answer. Chester clenched his fist,
‘WHO AM I IMMOLESS?’

‘Oh, she is a sweet one,’ a voice sang from the shadows of the cellar, ‘sweet. I can smell her blood from here. I can smell her body. I can smell her cunt!’ The sound of buzzing accompanied the voice. Archie lowered his head and watched as the figure danced forward.

The figure was tall and wore a black suit, black waistcoat, top hat, burgundy silk scarf, black gloves, wire-rimmed glasses and a silver neck chain with a ruby pendant dangling from it. His black cloak with a plush burgundy interior swished about him as he skipped into the dim light and waltzed around Charmaine. His hands joined in the merriment as the dental drill that he held provided the percussion to a little song he had composed,
‘Give me an eyeball, a chop to cut,
Couldn’t keep your trap shut.
You shall offer your chunky gut,
One limb or two,
Maybe four or three.
We'll boil the pot,
We'll stir the brew,
Then gather round.
For a ghastly stew.
A pinch of toe,
A finger free,
And we shall all have tea.’

Allyra shuddered,
‘I can’t remember who you are, Master.’
Chester pawed her hair, his eyes whitened, then flashed green,
‘Remember me.’
‘I can’t.’
‘You can, Immoless. Who am I?’

Once Nicolai-Nicolas ‘Demus’ Nicodemus, DDS, PhD, PhD, PhD, MB, BS, had completed his melodic pre-med, he gave his nurse, well Archie as he did not have a nurse, an issue he soon hoped to remedy, instructions,
‘Stuff her mouth with your scarf, then gag her.’
‘I’m not putting my scarf in there!’ Archie snapped, ‘I don’t know where she has been.’
Nicodemus rolled his blue eyes,
‘Fine!’ He searched his pocket and pulled out a very used burgundy handkerchief that carried the weight of green, red, white, and strangely yellow stains, ‘Use this, and…’ he pulled off his belt, ‘This.’
‘Your belt?’ Archie asked.
‘Don’t need it. I have been overindulging in tribute recently, I think it’s the thought of Nicolas finding us a bride.’
Archie nodded, taking the belt, and tenuously clasping the edge of Demus’s handkerchief.
‘I know that feeling.’ He replied, then quickly stuffed the handkerchief, that he was glad to see the back of, into Charmaine’s mouth and looped the belt about her face to stop the emittance of any irritating noises.
‘Now, wake her!’ Demus instructed.

‘You are…’ Allyra whispered.
‘Yes?’ Chester replied.
‘You are… I don’t know, Chester. I can’t remember.’
‘Sink deeper,’ Chester whispered, ‘I have told you before, you do know.’

Charmaine was not overly happy about her situation. She could barely breathe under the weight of the straps and knew exactly why she was in her current predicament. Archie loomed over her grinning like a cheshire cat, a trick he had learned from Chester. Charmaine cast her eyes about the cellar. A strange man with black wavy hair and a matching suit was dancing about her sharpening a bone saw. To make matters worse, her mouth tasted of contaminated stale sweat, a taste she knew well on account of licking her own armpits when she woke late and had no time to wash.

‘Deeper,’ Chester whispered, ‘Who am I?’
‘You are Nicolas DeSilva, Master.’
‘Do you love me?’
‘You have ordered me to love you.’
Chester’s stomach lurched. Nicolas’s stomach lurched, even though he was not present. Her words hurt and Nicolas would not forget it.

Nicodemus held the bone saw above Charmaine’s head, grinning with an insane and toothy smile for far longer than was necessary. Charmaine was so focused on the saw that she quite neglected to notice Archie who was pulling a rusty scalpel from the trolley. Charmaine’s attention did, however, rapidly switch from Demus to Archie when the first incision was made in her chunky thigh.

Demus did not move. He remained fixed in a dancing posture, grinning with only his teeth whilst staring at their strapped victim.

Archie wielded the scalpel with enthusiasm. The blade was dragged around the flesh just above her knee. Archie then revisited the wound with extra pressure cutting to the bone. He drew a shallow cut from her wound to the top of her thigh where another incision was made, and another deeper track dug. Archie dipped the blade into the cut and tore a matching gash from one wound to the other. He dug his hand into the vertical incision and slowly peeled the flesh from around her thigh. Charmaine bit into Demus’s handkerchief and screamed through the gag, but the muzzle held well.

Archie’s trajectory was, however interrupted by another sound a BZZZZ then another BZZZZZ as Demus’s hand ‘accidentally’ lowered the dental drill. It pierced through the gag driving into one of Charmaine’s upper incisors,
‘Ooops,’ Demus smiled.
Archie shook his head and completed unpeeling the Charmaine thigh-roll until the bone was exposed. Demus’s drill bounced on the incisor again.

‘D? As in DeSilva?’ Smythe asked, dribbling onto the quill that he pressed against his lips.
‘D as in D.’
‘Got it!’ Smythe replied, then lowered the quill, missed the damp parchment that stuck to the desk entirely and wrote on the desk itself whilst dictating to himself,
‘Allyra DeSilva. Is that Mrs?’
‘Ms Allyra Cavidini D,’ Allyra hissed.
Smythe nodded,
‘Mrs Allyra DeSilva. Address?’
‘Tempus Cottage, Thanata.’
‘Corax Asylum, Togaduine. What can we do for you?’ Smythe asked.
‘You could start by writing my details down properly.’

Smythe tutted, shook his head in disgust, and turned to Hector,
‘What is the problem here apart from the usual hysterical woman syndrome?’
‘I’m right here!’ Allyra snapped.
Hector stroked her back,
‘Calm down.’
‘DON’T touch her!’ Smythe shouted suddenly, then leapt forward. His hand grasped Allyra’s wrist as he leaned over the desk and his eyes flashed red, causing Hector to relinquish his own hand and nod. Smythe locked eyes with Allyra and he held her gaze for several aching minutes before calming down and returning to his station.
‘Now,’ Smythe resumed, ‘symptoms?’
‘She wakes up in the sea,’ Hector began.
Smythe continued using the desk as a means to record the personal and data protected patient information,
‘Thinks she’s a fish.’
‘I don’t,’ Allyra interrupted, stroking her wrist to soothe the imprint of Smythe’s fingers.
‘Argumentative and hysterical. Anything else, HECTOR?’
‘I find her in the sea every morning. She has these turns you see. She usually seems confused, maybe a little drunk, and she has been having troubling dreams.

‘Alcoholic with delusions, confusion, lucid dreams and a sex addiction,’ Smythe noted.
Allyra leaned across the desk,
‘No one mentioned the sex addiction.’
‘And paranoid!’ Smythe concluded, ‘Now, tell me about these dreams.’

‘I dream that something throws me into the sea, always at the same spot, the cliffs of Thanata close to the coves. I hit the water. Then he comes. This monster, with eight eyes and long green locks of hair. He drags me down under the water and into a cave. We sit there, sometimes for hours. He whispers to me about the sea and about other things, maybe a wedding feast, but I never recall exactly what he says.’
Shiverton Smythe nodded and tapped her hand in a pseudo-comforting manner,
‘In your dreams, do you have any sexual encounters with this… Monster?’
Allyra blushed and Smythe’s tap turned into a stroke, one that she rather enjoyed. Their eyes locked again and Smythe offered a slight smile,
‘I am a doctor, Madam, there is no need to be ashamed.’
‘Yes. Yes, he makes love to me.’

Dr Smythe nodded and abruptly removed his hand,
‘Frantic sex under the waves with unusual sea-life. I conclude that you have a sex addiction and low iron levels, and to treat such an addiction one feeds it.’
Allyra shook her head,
‘That doesn’t sound right.’
‘Are you a doctor?’
‘No.’
‘Then let me do my job. I shall demonstrate.’

Smythe rummaged about in the pockets of his coat pulling out bloodied scalpels, strangely brown thermometers, a toenail, the odd eyeball, a kidney, and finally a syringe filled with bright green, glowing fluid. He left the nasty debris on the desk shoving it as close to Allyra as possible, then tipped forward, opened his mouth as his face elongated, and squirted half of the fluid in. He then injected the remainder into his arm. His eyes shone fluorescent emerald, and he let out a loud laugh.

Allyra leaned into Hector pleading,
‘Can we go, please?’
Hector shook his head,
‘I told you. Eccentric.’
Dr Smythe laughed again and continued to do so until his eyes reverted to their usual green. He then waved the syringe in Allyra’s face,
‘Do you want some?’
‘No thank you.’ Allyra replied, ‘I do not want some!’
‘I suggest you enjoy your little addiction and then you might stop hurling yourself into the sea!’
‘I don’t…’ Allyra began, but Dr Smythe ignored her and drowned her voice out with his own claptrap,
‘And I am going to refer you to Nicolai Dr Otto Von Riesigerschwanz.’
Allyra’s face brightened and she fidgeted with excitement, so much excitement that she forgot to ask what a Nicolai was,
‘Dr Riesigerschwanz?’ She grinned.
Smythe grunted,
‘Fan, are you?’
‘Oh, very much so. I have read Bringing Back Masculinity, The Art of Feminine Surrender and am now reading 1000 Uses for Cucumbers You Never Thought Of. He is very enlightening.’

Dr Smythe sniffed something grey and furry that had been sitting between his fingers for a few weeks,
‘I am glad you like pop-psychology trash. I shall ask Nicolas to arrange an appointment with Dr Dick at his earliest convenience.’
Allyra blinked twice,
‘Nicolas who?’
‘Oh my,’ Smythe said, directing his concern to Hector, ‘she is confused.’ He then tilted his head sadly in Allyra’s direction, ‘Nicolas DeSilva, Mrs DeSilva, your husband.’
Allyra shook her head,
‘You have me mistaken for someone else.’
‘No, you are just delusional. We spoke about this before.’
‘I never met you until today.’

Smythe ignored Allyra’s protests and pulled a slice of parchment from below the kidney that had been crawling up and down under Allyra’s nose, then dipped his quill in the mouldy red ink pot that sat on the desk,
‘Full disclosure Mrs DeSilva, I shall read you my referral letter as I write it, so you are fully aware.’ He turned back to Hector, ‘We cannot dismiss patients just because they are insane.’
‘I’m not insane!’ Allyra argued, forcing Smythe to shout her down once again!

‘DEAR NICOLAS,

Your wife presented today thinking she was a sex-mad fish. Possibly fornicating with sea-life, probably delusional, and quite mad. Suggest referral to Dr Dick and have Nicolai-Demus check her for any physical problems that may be upsetting her woman hormones.

See you soon,
Shiverton.’

Smythe folded the envelope, stuck the ends together with something green and globulous from his mouth and clicked his fingers.
‘Disgusting!’ Allyra muttered.
‘Pardon me?’ Smythe snapped.
‘Nothing.’
‘I should think so too!’

Smythe clicked his fingers a second time and a giant albatross opened the door, lifted itself from the ground, then swooped onto the desk. Allyra moved back to accommodate its huge form. Smythe raised an eyebrow,
‘It’s Nicolai-Bigglesworth’s bird. We work with what we have!’ The doctor explained, without really clarifying anything, ‘Now, it has been nice to see you again Allyra and we look forward to you coming home to Corax.’

Allyra’s eyes widened,
‘No! Listen, I don’t live at Corax, so you can’t very well look forward to me coming home to your weird asylum.’
‘Yes, indeed we do. We all look forward to it immensely,’ Smythe then lowered his chin and shifted his gaze to Hector, ‘she has really lost it this time. Nicolas will be most upset.’
Allyra leaned back in her chair,
‘You’re a spy for Nicolas?’ She smirked.
Smythe shook his head and let out a deep, exhausted sigh,
‘Don’t be absurd woman. I have just made a referral to two doctors who happen to be resident at Corax. Surely you don’t expect such brilliant minds to operate from the sordid mire of Ashurrel Hospital?’ Smythe did not wait for an answer but moved swiftly to Allyra’s second issue, ‘Now, iron levels. Probably one of the underlying causes of your turns. Shall we address that?’

Allyra nodded with a little more hope than most would have in such a situation.
‘Good!’ Smythe smiled. He then removed the syringe that had been dangling from his tricep, pushed and pulled the plunger up and down, then dug it into the crook of the same arm. The needle was a little confused, and it took some time to locate the vein. Smythe repeatedly pulled the plunger up and down for a little while, allowing Allyra to glance a show of his dark red, and occasionally blue, blood as it danced in and out of the poorly attached tube. Finally, the blood opted to remain in the tube, and Smythe yanked the needle out,
‘That was fun, wasn’t it?’ The doctor asked.

Allyra ignored Smythe and stood, desperately trying not to look unsettled,
‘Thank you doctor. Thank you, Hector. I am going now.’
‘Wait!’ Dr Smythe shouted loudly, for no particular reason. Allyra stood still. Smythe climbed onto his desk and crawled across it, dragging his hulking form over the debris and parchment. He then knelt, pulling his body to its full height, and slathered a dirty great lick up Allyra’s cheek. A second lick followed. Allyra grimaced. As her hand rose to wipe away the slime Smythe slammed the needle into her arm and pressed the plunger forcing his blood into her vein,
‘Ow, what the fuck?’ Allyra yelled.
Smythe cupped her face in his gnarly hands and lowered his right ear to his shoulder, then dropped his head to the other shoulder,
‘We need you,’ he said softly. His lips brushed hers, and Allyra shuddered. Time stood still, at least for a while, then the spell was broken.

Smythe twisted the needle out at an angle and licked her blood from the tip whispering,
‘Now you may go.’

Scene III: The Spider and His Fly

The 1stDay of the 4th Moon, 1536 P.V.
Corax Asylum, Togaduine

Nicolas had been waiting patiently in his chambers for the return of Stacia, the first Immoless of the century, all day. She had escaped during a rather eventful night after Nicolas wilfully left her cell door open. His patience was wearing thin, so he penned an urgent letter to the Nicolai known as Chester, Nicolai-Chester, that read,
‘Ches,
Hoe number one has escaped. A free lick to anyone who can retrieve her. Give the third Immoless one from me,
Nicolas.’

Stacia was a blonde, plain sort of priestess, or rather, Immoless, with the personality of a turnip, and the intelligence to match. Nicolas had found her a little too whiny and rapidly became bored of taunting her cunt with hot irons as she was really no fun at all.

He allowed two of his Nicolai, namely Nicolai-Commodore Bigglesworth, the Purple Pirate of The Getsug Sea and Nicolai-Mr Dibble, a lion tamer from the made-up organisation The International Union of Circi of the DeSilva Group, who both resembled Nicolas with auburn-brown shaggy hair, piercing green eyes, a constant stubble and a mandatory dribble of blood about their chins, to waterboard Stacia for several hours.

They too grew bored with her whining. Screaming was one thing, but a monotonous whine proved quite irritating and did nothing for anyone’s libido.

Mr Dibble lost interest early on in the session and moved from the torture chambers to the cells to inflict his presence on a new tribute, a red-head named Ariadne. Mr Dibble was fascinated as to why Ariadne’s parents insisted on giving her a spider’s name, and it was something he raised whilst thrusting his cock into her from behind as she stood chained against the cell wall,
‘Madam,’ his deep, alpha voice growled, ‘I should like you to impart the history of your proper noun and its relation to the lineage of the arachnid community.’ Dibble was nothing if not romantic.

Ariadne, who was raised to serve, had not benefitted from any form of classical education. She was not even forced into The Deep’s diabolical thesapien education system. The range of her education consisted of basic language skills, classes in how to submit to the Immortalis, and lessons in dying with dignity, whilst, of course, pleasing the men. No one had discussed grammar or the history and culture of arachnids with her at any point in her short life.

Ariadne shrugged, whispering,
‘I don’t understand.’ This infuriated Mr Dibble forcing him to thrust harder, as it demonstrated yet again that the quality of tribute livestock was in massive decline. After a few minutes, and without blowing his load, he removed his cock and watched Ariadne tremble.

Mr Dibble adjusted his red and black top hat, and fiddled with its silver hanging embellishments and plumage, then prowled around his victim,
‘Your name, Madam, Ariadne. Is it not a spider’s name?’
Ariadne was not sure how to answer, so to prevent further irritation she simply replied,
‘Yes.’
This pleased Mr Dibble. ‘No’ was not a word recognised by the Nicolai.

Mr Dibble looked over the tribute. She was fairly clean, a sure sign that she was new, as Nicolas discouraged cleanliness in tributes. However, she wore a torn and bloodied white dress, and there were dried blood stains about her thighs and bite marks about her neck suggesting that Nicolas had eagerly taken the first serving.

The tributes were always damaged by the time the Nicolai took their turns. There was a clear hierarchy. Within that hierarchy Nicolas came first, second and third, literally, and as loudly as possible. In Nicolas’s mind this loud performance signalled some failing on the part of the older tributes who no longer made him cry out. This, he believed, caused the older tributes great jealousy. It did not. They were simply quite happy that someone else was suffering his attentions for a change.

Mr Dibble lifted and spun his cane. All of the Nicolai held a cane with a skull on the top, except for Nicolai-Demize who was only a head. Mr Dibble removed the cap at the base of the cane and used the blade that jutted out to rip Ariadne’s gown. To his great disappointment, Ariadne was not spider-like at all. She only had four limbs, and to make matters worse, she unequivocally refused to hide the fact that she only had two eyes. There were no fangs either.

Mr Dibble ripped the dress from her body and inspected her carefully, inside and out, for hidden clues of arachnitism. He even used a speculum, torch and eyepiece to ensure the search for signs of arachnitism extended to all sneaky orifices. There were no spider-like indicators, however she did have two beautiful supple breasts which he hoped to examine more closely.

Mr Dibble licked his lips and spun Ariadne around, breaking both chained arms with a loud crack. This caused a massive scene. Ariadne started screaming, and in response the other inmates began to cheer, roar or cry. This strengthened Mr Dibble’s resolve, among other things, and, without hesitation, he pushed her back up against the wall and entered her without mercy.

Ariadne was not a virgin, not anymore. Mr Dibble presumed that her insides were most likely filled with salty residue as Nicolas had made such a show of his interaction with Ariadne earlier in the night that the whole asylum were privy to the noise.

Once Nicolas had finished, Chester quickly followed, and shamed Ariadne with his wily tongue, and prolific flute before going about his business. Chester and Ariadne enjoyed the coupling so much and were both moaning so loudly that they barely noticed Chives, Nicolas’s skeletal henchman, changing the sheets during their interaction. Chives replaced the filthy sheets with filthier sheets as only Nicolas was privileged with some level of hygiene. Not much, as he was not a fan of it, but more than the Nicolai or the tributes ever received.

Unlike Nicolas and Chester, Mr Dibble had nothing to prove. He was just there for a quick snack. He drove in and out of Ariadne at speed, whilst she continued to complain about her arms. This only progressed his excitement, and he came quickly. As he came his fangs sunk into her shoulder. The blood poured freely, so he lapped at it, before biting into her mouth and cheek, tearing out a few hearty chunks of flesh.

The Nicolai were not concerned about the presentation of used tributes; their only concern was feeding their own needs. A hole in the cheek or a missing lip made no difference to the overall experience. If anything, it heightened their arousal. Ariadne proved highly unsatisfying to Mr Dibble, having no arachnid qualities, proving to be as thick as a plank, and expressing herself through the most dreadful, grating squeals. All in all, the experience was a disappointment.

Bigglesworth was not having much luck either. Stacia’s noisy whines grew highly irritating, forcing poor Bigglesworth to leave longer and longer gaps between her drowning and him reviving her. Eventually he untied her and dragged her back down the stairs, by her hair, to her cell. Stacia’s cell was a few cells along from Ariadne’s cage. On arrival, Bigglesworth quickly threw Stacia in and double locked the door.

Both Bigglesworth and Mr Dibble retired to the south wing for the night, leaving Nicolas to roam the halls in an acute state of boredom.

The sobs of Stacia and the cries of Ariadne intercepted his path. Nicolas halted his rhythmic pace, his long ears twitched and a smile scarred his blood-soaked lips. He stopped in front of a mirror and adjusted his orange and green lounge suit, which had not one day prior been torn by an ungrateful tribute, and glared at his magnificent reflection.

Nicolas’s eyes flashed from green to brown, then back again. Then one turned blue, wandered around for a while, slithered into his head and returned to its original position quite green. Nicolas adjusted his tall top hat so that his long greasy hair clung about his slimy neck. A few flies formed a buzzing fan club about his being. He did not waft them away since they often paid him a visit.

Nicolas then moved closer to the mirror, tilting his head from one side to the other as his eyes rolled up and down. Once satisfied with his appearance, he danced from the entrance hall of the asylum to the cells.

The cells were housed on the ground floor, and the tributes allocated cages according to preference. Nicolas’s favourites were placed closest to the entrance hall and his office. This made life easier for Nicolas and gave the Nicolai a clear architectural layout of tribute hierarchy. The basement, for want of a better word, housed the dungeons where the vampires were kept. Nicolas liked to believe that the dungeons were a worse option than the cells, but the two prisons were just as revolting as each other.

All cages, whether cells or dungeons, comprised of filthy walls, an excess of damp and mould, chains and cuffs, a bed with blood-soaked, and otherwise soiled sheets, facilities tucked away behind a partition so Nicolas did not have to look at them, and an unusual flooring system laden with dubious wooden planks, pipes for sole burning and bare wires for electrocution purposes.

The generosity of providing a bed was for Nicolas’s comfort, and the straps and handcuffs were to ensure his prey did not ruin his indulgences by fidgeting, squirming and generally complaining. He even had gags on standby for the more vocal tributes and any inmates who objected to his passions. Nicolas did not care whether they objected or not but did not want the bother of fighting for what was his ordained right as an Immortalis.

Nicolas danced to Ariadne’s cell first. She had proven quite entertaining earlier in the night, so he could not fathom what she was carrying on about. He did not ask her either, largely because he did not care. He danced outside of her cell for a few minutes, then scraped his cane up and down the bars. Ariadne paid him no attention. She had not been in Corax long enough to understand the etiquette expected by Nicolas, and the other inmates did not warn her as it amused them to see newbies get a good beating.

Nicolas attempted to seduce her with his strange and largely uncoordinated dance again. His gangly legs jolted up and down, and his arms twisted into eerie theatrical contortions. Still Ariadne was unmoved.

Nicolas stopped dancing and shoved his face between two of the bars,
‘What ails you, Madam?’ Nicolas asked.
Ariadne shook her head, and twisted her arms against the chains, which only caused further discomfort. She winced and sniffed. Nicolas grew impatient,
‘I said what is wrong?’
Ariadne pursed her lips, then sobbed,
‘My arms.’
Nicolas widened his eyes and lowered his chin,
‘Is it… Very painful?’ He smiled.
Ariadne nodded. Nicolas pushed himself away from the bars, positively glowing,
‘Why didn’t you say so?’ His smile drifted into a smirk, ‘I have just the thing... CHIVES! CHIVES!’ His bellowing perforated the entire wing. Chives rapidly hobbled to him from the darkness at the far end of the corridor,
‘You muttered something, Sir?’
Nicolas skipped about in a circle,
‘Yes Chives, get me a chair. Our fine tribute is in pain and needs diagnosis and treatment immediately.’
With that, Nicolas danced back up the corridor and disappeared. Chives hobbled after him.

The tributes, like the immolesses, were largely ill-prepared for any interaction with the Immortalis. An agreement had been made after The War Before the Dusk, between the Electi, the DarkBadb, and the local lords, that any preparation or honest information about the Immortalis and their antics may cause upset among the prey, or risk the sort of exposure that no bureaucracy wants.

It was agreed that talk of torture, death, cannibalism, and the like may result in civil unrest. No party wanted that as it would impact taxation and spending. As such, neither the tributes nor the immolesses were told of the true horrors that awaited them. Instead, the Immortalis were depicted as brooding, darkly seductive vampires, and their habits highly romanticised as a sensual ritual. Unlike the tributes, the immolesses were aware that no one survived the Immortalis giving a more grounded understanding of the death cult that they had been born into. This dashed their hopes. However, the tributes arrived living in dreamland. This suited Nicolas as it made their suffering all the more entertaining.

Chives returned with a chair. It was more a throne than a chair. A magnificent creature carved from the finest Ashurrel oak and painted in yellow and black plaid. To the average person it would perhaps be deemed tacky, but to Nicolas it was a reminder of how important he was.

Nicolas arrived soon after Chives. He was no longer dancing but marching with an air of professional arrogance. A pair of round spectacles sat atop his nose, and he carried a large book, quill and inkpot. Chives placed yellow and black cushions on his chair and even pulled it out for Nicolas for no reason in the world.

Nicolas sat down, rested his utensils on the arm of the chair, and made a huge gesture of wriggling, clasping and cracking his fingers,
‘Shall we begin?’
Ariadne had no idea what was happening but nodded in the hope that he may attend to the raw throbbing sensation stifling both of her arms and causing a sickness in her belly.

Nicolas opened the book and placed it on his lap. He dipped the quill into the dark red ink, forced a cough, and then presented the first question,
‘What is your name?’
‘Ariadne,’ Ariadne answered, knowing that Nicolas knew her name full well as he had placed a name holder card on her cell door for the Nicolai.
Nicolas peered over his glasses,
‘And your surname?’
‘I don’t know what that is.’ Ariadne replied.
Nicolas tutted,
‘Chives, fetch another chair, and send for Dr Von Riesigerschwanz.’
Chives nodded, causing his skeletal neck to crunch and crack,
‘Very good, Sir.’
‘And don’t pretend you can’t see Dr Dick. If you are in that sort of a mood, get the porters to send for him.’
‘As you say, Sir!’ Chives replied, then limped back towards the main hall.

Nicolas looked down at his book and began to write whilst muttering just loud enough for Ariadne to hear,
‘Does not know who she is.’
‘I do know who I am,’ Ariadne argued.
Nicolas shook his head and continued to scribe,
‘Argumentative.’

The red head in the next cell, who, according to her name label, was known as Zena, sniggered. Nicolas dropped his gaze and looked over his glasses at her,
‘Do you want to be next?’
Zena shook her head and retreated from the bars.
‘I thought not!’ Nicolas snorted, then returned to his diagnosis, ‘Now. Who did this to you?’
Ariadne hesitated forcing Nicolas to command her to speak. This annoyed him,
‘Speak up, woman!’
‘You did, Sir.’
Nicolas’s lower jaw dropped, and he shook his head,
‘Me? Me? Madam, I have done no such thing. I visited you earlier. I was courteous. We had some fun, but I never broke your arms.’
‘Are they broken?’ Ariadne asked in panic, then the tears came. Nicolas hated tears,
‘No, we are not starting that. Let’s stick to the facts, no amateur dramatics and no waterworks. Let’s try again. Who did this to you?’
Ariadne trembled and shivered.
‘Today please!’ Nicolas snapped, as his patience thinned.
‘You, Sir.’
‘And how was I dressed?’
‘Like a ringmaster, Sir.’
Nicolas let out a low laugh, then drew his attention back to his book,
‘Delusions.’ He looked up at her slowly, his eyes practically glowing, ‘And possible hallucinations.’

Nicolas’s train of thought was interrupted by Chives heaving another chair up the corridor accompanied by the clicking of Nicolai-Dr Riesigerschwanz’s boots. Dr Riesigerschwanz, a prolific psychiatrist, psychoanalyst and writer, was well-known throughout The Deep for his revered work on the power of masculinity. He had several best-sellers including 1000 Uses for Cucumbers you Never Thought of, Bringing Back Masculinity, The Art of Feminine Surrender, and Nicolas’s favourite,

text:
🇺🇸 MASTER CHIEF CARL BRASHEAR: A LEGACY OF COURAGE AND DETERMINATION

Born on January 19, 1931, in Tonieville, Kentucky, Carl Brashear joined the U.S. Navy in 1948 and became its first Black diver in 1954, overcoming racial discrimination and countless obstacles.

In 1966, while helping recover a lost hydrogen bomb off the coast of Spain, Brashear suffered a devastating injury while protecting a fellow sailor. His left leg was eventually amputated below the knee.

The Navy offered him medical retirement.

He refused.

Through extraordinary determination, he learned to dive with a prosthetic leg and returned to active diving duty in 1968.

In 1970, he became the Navy's first Black master diver, achieving the highest enlisted diving qualification.

He retired in 1979 after 31 years of honorable service. His remarkable life later inspired the film Men of Honor.

Master Chief Carl Brashear passed away on July 25, 2006, at the age of 75. He was laid to rest at Woodlawn Memorial Gardens in Norfolk, Virginia, with full military honors.

“It's not a sin to get knocked down, it's a sin to stay down.”

Master Chief Carl Brashear proved that courage isn't measured by the obstacles we face, but by our determination to overcome them.

Fair winds and following seas, Master Chief. Your legacy lives on. 🇺🇸🫡

text:
Chapter 3 – Trials at Florissant.
.
In 1821, the little community of Florissant sent out its first offshoot. With the consent and approbation of her Superior General, Mother Barat, Mother Duchesne made her second foundation in Lower Louisiana, as it was then called, at a place known as Grand Coteau, in the Opelousas region. Mother Eugénie Audé and Sister Mary Layton were sent to begin it. A little later, Mother Duchesne was able to send them valuable help in the person of Madame Xavier (Anna) Murphy, who had just arrived from France with Madame Lucile Mathevon, another valiant woman, who had a notable part to play in the early history of the Society of the Sacred Heart in America.
.
The school at Grand Coteau had soon filled up, but ere long Mother Duchesne heard of the distressing condition to which the new community was reduced, through sickness and overwork. With the uncalculating charity that characterized her, she at once determined to go in person to their assistance, though it was in the middle of summer and the journey must necessarily be long and painful, as well as expensive. She took with her Madame Saint Cyr and a lay novice to leave at Grand Coteau, and Therese Pratte, whose family had so hospitably entertained her and her companions during their two weeks’ stay in Saint Louis, after their arrival. The young girl was one of her pupils, who had obtained her father’s consent for a visit to Mother Audé.
.
The voyage was long, full of difficulties and endless interruptions and delays, and marked by very dramatic and even tragic incidents, especially on the return trip, of which alone we will give a brief account. Among other particulars, she had to go from Plaqumine all the way down to New Orleans to find a boat for Saint Louis. In New Orleans she was stricken with malarial fever, still the physician advised her departure by the first steamer, because at the time yellow fever was epidemic in the city. Scarcely, however, had the steamer started on her voyage, before the dread disease broke out on board, the captain being the first to die of it. Mother Duchesne, though reduced to a state of great prostration, gathered up the remnant of her strength to take care of one of the yellow fever patients on board, to whom no one else seemed to give any attention. She not only ministered to his needs, but converted and baptized him before he died.
.
Weak and exhausted as she was, foreseeing that under the existing conditions the steamer would scarcely be able to reach her destination, she determined to trust in Providence, and land with her young companion at Natchez. But the quarantine excluded her from the town, nor would any one in the neighborhood take them in, for fear of the prevailing epidemic. Providence came to their assistance, for, as they sat by the river bank upon their trunks, alone and friendless, a young man chanced to pass by, and seeing them so forlorn, offered his services and went in search of shelter for them. Soon he found an honest German who willingly took them in, but he had no bed to offer them, except the one in which his wife had died of yellow fever a fortnight previously, and of which not even the sheets had been changed. From this place Mother Duchesne found means of making her distress known to the Abbé Maenhaut, Curé of the church in the town, and in later years Rector of the Cathedral of New Orleans. He came promptly to her assistance, and had her removed to the hospitable home of a family of the name of Davis. Complete rest and change of air restored her health, and in a few weeks she reembarked for Saint Louis on the steamer Cincinnati. On their way up they passed by a steamboat tied up and partially wrecked, in charge of three men. It was the Hecla, the boat from which she had landed at Natchez. Then it was that she could see how providential had been the change she had made. The yellow fever had continued its ravages on the unfortunate boat, and on a little island nearby could be seen the graves of thirteen of its victims. Moreover, the boilers had exploded and several men had been severely injured. At last, after another delay of two weeks, caused by the grounding of the Cincinnati, Mother Duchesne and her companion reached Saint Louis, after an absence of five months. The account of this terrible journey contained in Mother Duchesne’s letters to Mother Barat is such as might come from the pen of a saint. There is not a word of complaint, and no regrets for herself, save for the Communions and Masses she had lost.
.
On her return to Florissant she found the school greatly diminished and in a state of insubordination; this latter condition prevailed not only among the pupils, but also among the orphans, of whom she always had several in the house, and whom she educated and provided for entirely. Her firm hand soon reestablished order, but it was not in her power to remove what had been the cause of the state of disturbance, in which she had found the school. The times were very hard; there was little money in circulation, and Bishop Dubourg had been obliged to borrow in order to finish his new cathedral, which the rapid increase of the population rendered necessary. The great bishop’s administrative ability was above question, but the resources he had counted upon failed him, through the dishonesty of an agent, and this, with the difficulty of the times, made it impossible for him to meet his obligations; while his creditors, finding themselves in much the same situation, were clamorous against him, breaking out into abuse and menaces. They were even threatening to seize his residence and have it sold for their benefit.
.
As a matter of course, Mother Duchesne and her community shared largely in the odium that had fallen upon Bishop Dubourg. She was afflicted, but chiefly on account of the indignities offered to the great missionary prelate, and the harm done to religion by the nature of the difficulties in which he found himself involved. After a time the storm subsided, leaving, however, in the public mind a feeling of rancor and resentment, one of whose effects was a settled enmity with regard to Mother Duchesne and her community. Soon, of the pupils left to her, there were only two whose schooling was being paid for. Still her courage and her reliance upon God never wavered, and her confidence was rewarded. She does not say how it happened, but she affirms that she was never less pinched by poverty than at this time. She met this crisis in her usual heroic fashion. Disregarding the idle talk of which she was the subject, she refused to dismiss any of the boarding pupils who were being educated gratis. She already had a free school for girls, and she opened another for boys, as also two classes, one for the poor women of the village and one for the grown-up girls.
.
And how, with such scanty resources, did she manage to make both ends meet? By her own thrift and ingenious industry, which enabled her to turn the least trifle to account, with an occasional remittance of a few hundred francs from her relatives, and such assistance as Mother Barat could spare out of her own penury. But her surest asset was her confidence in Divine Providence, which always came to her assistance, often in the most remarkable manner. With these she covered the expenses of her convent, extinguished by degrees her indebtedness, and at the same time was prodigal in her charity toward the missionaries, and very liberal toward the poor.
.
In the situation above described, Saint Louis was no place for Bishop Dubourg. Leaving in charge there his newly-consecrated coadjutor, Bishop Rosati, he took up his residence at a short distance above New Orleans. The last of the many benefits he had conferred upon Missouri was a foundation for a little company of Jesuit Fathers and scholastics, to whom he donated his farm at Florissant. They arrived just at this time, and on account of their connection with the prelate met with a cool reception from many of the people. This was another heavy affliction for Mother Duchesne, who felt that, in view of the good they could surely do in the country, neither she nor any one else could do too much for them. Their poverty was very great, and she did not hesitate to beg for them. The friends she still had left in Saint Louis responded generously to her appeal, and sent her whatever they could afford to give. From others, however, to whom she had recourse, she met with harsh refusals. She despoiled herself and her community of all she could manage to do without. She took care of the altar linen and vestments for their domestic chapel, and spent part of her nights mending and making clothes for them. In the beginning she sent them their meals already prepared, and later on she supplied them with many articles for their missionary outfit. In fact, the Jesuit Mission of Missouri might have perished at its birth had it not been for her fostering care. It was to her an immense joy to see the abundant fruits the zeal and devotedness of the Fathers soon began to reap in the country around, to the distance of a hundred miles and more. She considered it a priceless benefit to have their Superior, Father Van Quickenborne, as chaplain, and above all, as confessor for the community.
.
After the coming of the Jesuit Fathers, Bishop Rosati’s missionaries seldom made any stay at Florissant, but they were constantly passing through it to and from their missions, and Mother Duchesne continued to keep open house for them as heretofore.
Her apostolic longings for the work of the evangelization of the Indians had never died out, and great was her delight when, one day, Father Van Quickenborne brought her two little Indian girls, shyly hiding under his cloak, and asked her to take them and educate them. This was the beginning of the Indian school which, while it lasted, was the joy of her heart. However, it never counted more than twenty children, and came to an end in two years, the Indians being driven back further and further by the inflowing tide of white immigration.
.
Chapter 4 – Saint Michael’s Established.
.
In 1825, Mother Duchesne was called upon for another foundation. Father Delacroix, the predecessor of Father Van Quickenborne, as pastor of Florissant, was a holy and learned Belgian priest, whom Bishop Dubourg used to call his angel. He had the highest opinion of Mother Duchesne’s sanctity, and became a lifelong friend of hers. After leaving Florissant, he was stationed upon the Mississippi River, at a considerable distance above New Orleans. Before long, with the approbation of Bishop Dubourg, he asked for a foundation of the Religious of the Sacred Heart in his neighborhood. His petition was readily granted, and a location was chosen in the Parish of Saint James. To meet the first expenses of the building, the zealous pastor handed over eighteen thousand dollars, which he had collected for the purpose. This was the house known as Saint Michael’s. Mother Audé was its first Superior, and soon it was in as flourishing a condition as that of Grand Coteau.
.
Two years later, 1827, Father Neil, one of the resident pastors of Saint Louis and director of the college founded by Bishop Dubourg, asked for and obtained a foundation in that city. This was what Mother Duchesne, as well as Mother Barat, had been wishing for from the very beginning. Moreover, though Mother Duchesne had no idea of giving up Florissant, it was too distant from the city for convenience, and besides various other drawbacks, every rain flooded the convent grounds, greatly adding to the hardships endured by the nuns. She applied to Mr. John Mullanphy, a wealthy capitalist, asking him to sell her one of the houses he owned in Saint Louis, and he gave her one, with twenty-four acres of ground on the outskirts of the city, together with some assistance in money, on condition that she would, in perpetuity, keep twenty orphans. The house had the name of being haunted on account of the strange, unearthly noises heard in it, especially at night. That circumstance did not frighten Mother Duchesne, who soon discovered that the ghosts were nothing but cats that dropped down the chimneys to hold their nightly assemblies in the vacant rooms. On the first of May of that same year she took possession of the house with one companion, and remained there as Superior, leaving Mother Lucille Mathevon in her place at Florissant. The following year she had in her charge twelve boarders, ten orphans and forty day pupils, most of the latter having been received gratis.
Here, as elsewhere, her life was one of extreme poverty, privation and unremitting toil, to which, as she had always done, she added fasts, vigils and bodily penances, such as have rarely been equalled in the lives of the greatest canonized saints. She was often without a cent in the house, but this did not prove a bar to her charity. The poor never left the convent door empty handed, and the priests, most of whom were doing missionary work, and were as poor as herself, became the objects of her particular care. She supplied them with clothes, especially cassocks, that they might make a suitable appearance at the altar, and also altar linen and vestments, which she embroidered and made herself. During the first year of her stay in Saint Louis, her greatest privation, for herself and her community, was the lack of spiritual assistance. On week days they were often without Mass, and on such occasions Mother Duchesne would remain fasting until noon, in the hope that some priest might drop in to offer the Holy Sacrifice at a later hour, as it sometimes happened, or who at least, might give her Holy Communion.
.
In the meantime, the Jesuit Fathers had been making great headway, and they acquired a firm footing in Saint Louis, when Bishop Rosati handed over to Father Van Quickenborne, the head of the newly-organized Mission of Missouri, the college founded several years previously by Bishop Dubourg, and which, in the course of time, developed into the present Saint Louis University. But Father Van Quickenborne was replaced some months later in the office of Superior by Father Verhaegen, who had come with him from Maryland in 1823. In this same year, 1827, the latter founded a permanent mission at Saint Charles, and made it his headquarters. He also established, at the same place, a school for boys, and applied at once to Mother Duchesne to found one for girls. It seemed a rash undertaking to make two foundations in the same year, with such scanty resources in subjects and money; but what tempted her was the spiritual destitution of the people, who were all Catholics, and among whom the Protestants were busily at work. Mother Barat, tempted in the same way, gave her consent, and Mother Lucille Mathevon was placed in charge of the new house. It did a great deal of good, in spite of a long struggle with poverty and adversity.
.
Just a little before this time, at Bishop Rosati’s desire, Mother Duchesne, with Mother Barat’s approbation, had taken charge of the house of the Daughters of Charity, founded by the Father Nerinckx, near the head of the Bayou Lafourche, in the present State of Louisiana, and now threatened with extinction for want of vocations. The devoted prelate’s earnest request could not be refused, but the foundation was an unpromising one from the beginning, and a few years later it had to be closed.
The following year, 1828, as there were already six American houses, Mother Barat directed Mother Duchesne to assemble their superiors in a Provincial Council, in order to take measures for securing uniformity of action among them; and, to spare them the trouble of coming to her, Mother Duchesne went down to meet them at Saint Michael’s. After the Council she visited the houses in Louisiana, and was able, in her report to the Mother General, to give a very favorable account of them all except that of Lafourche where, to say nothing of other obstacles to success, the directions given by her in accordance with the intentions of Mother Barat, had not been understood or carried out.

text:
Venerable Philippine Duchesne, by G. E. M. Part 1
.
Preface.
.
There have been many heroic figures in the history of American Catholicity. The sowing of the faith in our beloved land was not accomplished lightly. Anguish of soul and weariness of body were required of our pioneers, no less than of those of other lands. Our predecessors in this portion of God’s vineyard left home and kindred and friends and cast themselves on a strange shore, wanderers for God’s cause, giving their lives in labor and anguish of spirit, that the glad tidings of salvation might be spread far and wide.
.
Some of these folk were martyrs in very truth. Through the mercy of Christ their heart’s blood has sanctified our soil. Others by living their length of days in the midst of privations and sorrows, that Christ might be known and glorified, fell little short of the martyrdom of blood itself. The memory of these still lives, enshrined in hearts that love them for their tireless zeal and their dauntless courage. Of such pioneers was the Venerable Philippine Duchesne, a truly valiant woman, to whom the American Church owes a debt of gratitude too great for payment.
.
The following pages are too few to give more than a glimpse of her heroic labors, but they have caught inspiration from their subject, and something, too, of her fragrant piety. No one will read them without admiration for one who was so weak and yet so strong, so humble, and yet so daring in work for God.
.
Mother Duchesne has a lesson for this age of softness and indolence. She has shown us the way to heroism and offers us motives for entering thereon. For this gratitude is due. This sketch is conceived in a spirit of thankfulness, a tribute of appreciation that will speak a clear, forceful message to sad hearts and selfish hearts and timorous souls, inspiring all with great ideals and holy ambitions to do a mite for the leader, Christ.
.
Chapter 1 – Volunteers for the American Missions.
.
In the early annals of the Catholic Church in this country, no name stands more preeminent than that of the Venerable Philippine Duchesne. She was one of the first, and altogether the greatest, among the spiritual daughters of the Blessed Madeleine Sophie Barat, so well known as the Foundress of the Society of the Sacred Heart. The pioneer of that Institute in the New World, it was in the midst of sorrow, and penury, and strenuous toil, that she cast the seed of the harvest whose plentiful sheaves are carried with joy by those who have come after her. She was a valiant cooperator in the work of the Catholic missionaries during the early part of the last century, and American Catholics can scarcely fail to be interested in her story.
.
She was born in Grenoble, France, 29 August 1769, the same year as Napoleon Bonaparte. Her father, Pierre François Duchesne, was a prosperous lawyer, practising in the Parliament, or law court of Grenoble, the capital of the Province of Dauphiny, while her mother, Rose Perrier, belonged to a family of wealthy merchants of the same city. Pierre François Duchesne had adopted the false teachings of Voltaire and his school, but his wife was very pious, and carefully brought up her children in the love and fear of God. Philippine was the next to the last in a family of six. From her earliest years she was noted for her serious turn of mind. One of her chief pleasures was reading, but even this had to be of a serious kind. Roman history was an especial favorite, but what she loved most of all was the lives of the saints, particularly the martyrs. Another of her pleasures was to assist the poor. All of her pocket money, with everything else that she could dispose of, went to them, and she loved to distribute her alms with her own hand.
At the age of twelve she was placed as a pupil at Sainte Marie d’en Haut, the Visitation Convent of her native city, to be prepared for her first Holy Communion. The remarkable spirit of prayer, of which she had given very early evidence, developed itself here, and her happiest moments were those she was permitted to spend in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament. A diligent and conscientious student, so ardent was her piety, that she was allowed by the kind nuns the privilege of making her morning meditation and reciting the Office in choir with them. The year after her admission into the school she made her First Communion, and it was on this happy occasion that she heard the call to a perfect life. Her parents, suspecting what was in her mind, removed her from the Convent. She silently acquiesced in this decision, keeping her own counsel, and continuing her studies with great success, in company with her cousins, the young Perfiers, who were afterward at the head of a great banking business in Paris, under the rule of the first Napoleon.
.
After four years of patient waiting, in the hope of obtaining her parents’ consent, and convinced at last that they never would grant it, she decided that it was time to act, and entered the novitiate of the Visitation. Her family became somewhat reconciled to her choice, after striving in vain to induce her to return home; but when the time for her profession came, her father absolutely forbade her to make it, on account of the dangerous political conditions of the time.
.
Four years later, in 1792, when the revolutionary storm was at its height, religious communities were being everywhere expelled from their homes, and Monsieur Duchesne withdrew his daughter from her convent, which was soon converted into a prison, and went to reside with his family in the Chateau of Granne, situated in a retired part of the country. By this time all her sisters were married, except the youngest, a child in her ‘teens; and when her mother was overtaken by her last illness, she it was who cared for her with devoted affection, and finally closed her eyes in death. After this the family possessions were divided among the children, and Philippine surrendered her share to the others, reserving only a small pension, barely sufficient for her needs.
.
This business being settled, she removed to a modest apartment in Grenoble, in order to be able to devote herself to works of mercy. Her ardent charity and intrepid energy found a wide field of action in those calamitous times. She visited and succored the unfortunate victims doomed to the guillotine, with whom the prisons were crowded. She ministered to the sick, and sought in their hiding places, the devoted priests who would not abandon their posts, to bring them to the bedside of the dying. She did all this at the constant risk of her life, often hearing sounds and witnessing sights that made her shudder with horror. As soon as the revolutionary storm had spent its fury somewhat, she was enabled to turn her attention to the neglected boys she found in the streets, assembling them in her own lodgings to teach them to read and write, and above all, to prepare them for the Sacraments.
At last, when the advent of Napoleon to power restored political and social order, Philippine Duchesne who, during all these years, had considered herself as irrevocably consecrated to the service of God, observing the rules and customs of the Visitation as closely as the adverse circumstances of the time would permit, resolved to reestablish in their old home the surviving members of the community of Sainte Marie d’en Haut, and resume a religious life with them. She obtained possession of the convent through the influence of her cousins, the Perriers, but her attempt to reorganize the community was not successful. In the meantime, however, several companions had gathered around her, forming a little community with the title of “Daughters of Faith,” under the direction of the Vicar General of Grenoble, the Abbé Rivet. This was in 1803 and the following year.
.
In the meantime, Madame Duchesne had heard, through the Abbé Rivet, of the Society of the Sacred Heart recently founded by Mother Madeleine Sophie Barat, under the guidance of Father Joseph Varin. It was through the latter that she applied for admission into the new Society. Father Varin, in reporting the case to the holy Foundress, declared that Madame Duchesne was a soul worth seeking for even to the end of the world. Lack of space does not permit us to dwell upon the beautiful humility, submission and childlike docility this valiant woman displayed in her intercourse with her new superior, who was ten years younger than herself, or her joy at finding herself under religious discipline and obedience. Nor can we stop to describe her heroic devotedness, zeal and charity toward all; her incredible activity, her self-immolation, the wonderful spirit of prayer that held her motionless the livelong night before the Tabernacle, when holy obedience allowed her the privilege.
.
The ten years that followed her profession were spent at Sainte Marie d’en Haut, toiling with an unflagging energy vivified and made fruitful by her intimate union with God. It was during that interval that the death of her father occurred. In his last illness, she surrounded him with the most loving care, and had the consolation of bringing him back to the faith of his baptism, and seeing him atone for the errors of a lifetime by a sincere repentance and an edifying end.
.
In the depths of her heart, Mother Duchesne had felt from the first an intense longing to devote herself to the evangelization of the barbarous tribes still sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death; but hitherto she had not seen any opening in that direction. So she was patient and put out her hands to all the strong things that Divine Providence placed in her way. One day, however, the illustrious Dom Augustin de Lestrange, Abbot of La Trappe, visited Sainte Marie d’en Haut, on his return from a tour among the North American missions. It was on the feast of Pentecost, a circumstance that did not escape the piety of Madame Duchesne; and the account he gave of the labors, dangers and fatigues endured by the missionaries in the New World, communicated a new and almost uncontrollable intensity to her apostolic yearnings. After this, she was possessed by one thought and one desire, that of devoting herself to the conversion of the savages of America. A few days later, she wrote to Mother Barat to tell her of Dom de Lestrange’s visit and of the ardent desires his discourses had aroused in her heart for the missions of America in particular. Mother Barat was delighted, but insisted that she must school herself to patience, until some providential opening should offer. For this she waited twelve long years, but with what burning desires, what tears and prayers! It would take too long to relate the circumstances which led to the visit of Mgr. Louis Valentin Dubourg, the newly consecrated Bishop of Louisiana, and describe the touching scene, when Mother Barat, in presence of the humble yet ardent entreaties of her strong-souled daughter, recognized the will of God, and gave the consent she implored, to let her have a share in the missionary labors of the zealous prelate in the far-off region of Louisiana.
.
In the hearts of God’s saints, joy and sorrow are in close alliance. Mother Duchesne was overwhelmed with joy on seeing the realization of her ardent and long-cherished desires; but a midnight blackness settled upon her soul, when she found herself about to sail away from the shores of sunny France, leaving behind her all that her loving heart held so dear, and with the conviction that the parting was final, as far as this life was concerned. But her strong spirit did not flinch for an instant, and the world would never have known how keenly she felt the sacrifice, were it not for a few lines in one of her letters to Mother Barat. Her companions were Madame Octavie Berthold, a fervent convert, whose father had been secretary to Voltaire; Madame Eugénie Audé, a young lady whose grace and elegance had been admired at the court of Savoy, and two lay sisters of tried virtue. After a tedious voyage of ten weeks in a small sailing vessel, they reached New Orleans on the Feast of the Sacred Heart, May 29, 1818, and as soon as it was possible, they set out for Saint Louis in one of the primitive steamboats of the time, a trip of six weeks, with numberless inconveniences and a very rough set of fellow-passengers.
.
Chapter 2 – First Schools in the New World.
.
Monsignor Dubourg cordially welcomed them to his Episcopal city, but the best he could do for them was to assign to them a log-house, which he had leased for their use at Saint Charles, a village on the Missouri River, at a distance of thirty miles from Saint Louis. Here they opened a boarding school which at first was only very scantily attended. They also opened a school for poor children, which immediately gathered in twenty-two pupils. As the nuns could not afford to keep a servant, they themselves had to cultivate the garden which, when they arrived, was a wilderness of weeds and briars. They also had to care for their cow and milk it, to chop wood for their fires, to bake their bread, to do the cooking and washing, besides teaching the two schools. For their supply of water, they were compelled to depend upon the muddy current of the Missouri River, brought to them in small bucketfuls, for which they had to pay an exorbitant price. The summer was very hot, and the cold of winter was so intense, that the clothes, hung up to dry near the kitchen stove, froze stiff. They had to be careful in handling the tin plates, etc., which served for their meals, lest their hands should adhere to them. The white fingers of Mesdames Audé and Berthold soon became hard and grimy. As for Mother Duchesne her hands had become rugged and horny long ago, from the hard, rough work to which she had devoted herself, especially after her reentrance into Sainte Marie d’en Haut. Indeed, it had always been her custom to reserve to herself, as much as possible, every kind of work that might be most painful or fatiguing for others. These particulars offer but a faint idea of the sufferings and privations endured by these refined and accomplished ladies, during those hard beginnings of the Society of the Sacred Heart in the New World.
.
During this trying time, Mother Duchesne’s desolation of heart was extreme, and her sense of loneliness indescribable. Whatever labors and austerities she had imposed upon herself hitherto, she had always had a circle of friends of the choicest kind and spiritual directors with whom she felt at her ease, but now all this was a thing of the past. Neither did she find any consolation in prayer. Her soul seemed dead within her, and yet, besides keeping up her own courage, she had to sustain that of her young companions, less inured to suffering and without her granite endurance. Still they were very brave and Bishop Dubourg could not but admire the valiant spirit and the cheerfulness of all.
.
But the establishment at Saint Charles was only a temporary arrangement to last for one year; and, as the house that was building at Florissant was not yet ready when the lease expired, Bishop Dubourg gave them the use of his farm near that village during the interval of waiting, with the log house upon it built by the consecrated hands of the bishop himself and of his heroic fellow missionaries. Toward the middle of September, 1819, followed by the intense regrets of the Abbé Richard, Curé of Saint Charles, and by the tears of the children of the free school, Mother Duchesne moved to the farm which had been thus placed at her disposal. The boarders, now increased to about twenty, accompanied them to their new home. Here one room and a garret was all that the nuns had for themselves and their pupils; but they had also a poor little chapel, where they were able to keep Him, who was the source of all their strength, and whose presence among them sweetened their life of toil and privation.
Mother Duchesne’s presence and supervision had hastened the work upon the new home, that was going up on a piece of ground given to them by the bishop; and by the end of December, it was sufficiently advanced to be habitable. Before leaving the farm, a great consolation was granted to the devoted nuns, in a retreat given by Father de Andreis, the saintly Lazarist missionary, who in 1900 was placed on the list of candidates for canonization. He cleared up Mother Duchesne’s perplexities on various points, and between those two kindred souls, there sprung up a holy friendship, which was for her a consolation and a support. Unfortunately, less than two years later, a malignant fever carried away this great servant of God, in the midst of his fruitful apostolic labors.
.
On Christmas Eve, the removal to the new house took place. Mother Duchesne and Audé were the last to leave the farmhouse, and it was late when they reached their destination, for they had made the entire way on foot, through deep snow, and in the face of a freezing wind. The little community set at once to the work of preparing their small and humble chapel for Midnight Mass, at which nuns and pupils, and also the workmen employed on the house, assisted and received Holy Communion. With regret we find ourselves compelled to pass over many interesting and touching particulars, such as the blessing and encouragement sent by the Sovereign Pontiff then reigning, the saintly Pius VII, and the gift of several relics and pictures from Bishop Dubourg, among the latter one that Mother Duchesne had greatly longed for, that of Saint Francis Régis, her special patron, whose name is so intimately connected with her own.
.
At Florissant, a new field was opened to her charity. Bishop Dubourg’s farm was intended by him as a quiet and healthful retreat, where his missionaries might, for a while, rest and refresh themselves after their toilsome apostolic journeys, or when their health required particular care. Madame Duchesne was a mother to them, furnishing them with their meals at any hour of the day, as they dropped in, often three or four at a time, washing and mending their clothes, and replacing them when needful, giving them the best of everything she had in the house. This occasioned a great deal of work and no small expense, and money was very scarce with her, to say nothing of the debts which had been incurred for the building of the house. But this valiant woman counted upon the Providence of God which never failed her, though its gifts were usually bestowed upon her so sparingly, as barely to keep her afloat. It was a great joy to her to help and serve the missionaries, and she declared that she would consider her life happy and well-spent, could she do nothing more than cook their meals for them. This generous hospitality was all the more heroic from the precarious condition of her own finances. Besides the debts, very heavy for the time, which were pressing upon her, and which she had been obliged to incur for the building of her house, a great business depression throughout the country reduced the number of her pupils, thus diminishing the small returns from the school, and, in 1820, a prolonged drought dried up the wells and compelled her to send to the river for all the water they needed.
Toward the end of 1820, when matters began to improve, the community was visited by sickness. Mother Duchesne’s turn came last, and so serious was her illness that it brought her to the verge of the grave. She recovered, however, and was able to resume her work at the end of two months.
.
It was just after this that vocations began to come in. The first were Emilie Saint Cyr, one of her pupils, and the sisters Eulalie and Mathilde Hamilton, of a very distinguished family related to the Fenwicks of Maryland, and also two lay sisters, Mary Layton and Mary Ann Summers. These five formed the nucleus of a novitiate whose numbers increased by degrees.
.

text:
Anthropic IPO;  Why I Sold My Anthropic $ANT IPO Shares at +32,5 % today? Cause Pure-Play AI Labs Are a $1.5T Trap  

I sold my $ANT IPO allocation right into today’s opening pop at $110 (+32.5%), minutes before it faded toward the low $90s. With all the hype you may wonder why? 

While I’m long-term bullish on AI, I see no viable standalone business case for pure-play ai labs like Anthropic at a $1.5T–$2T valuation. Let me explain, when i look at the underlying fundamentals, I expect that none of the standalone, pure-play AI labs will ultimately survive independently. Once their cash runs out without reaching sustainable profitability, and public markets are no longer willing to buy the dream or the hype, they will become prime takeover targets for established, cash-rich tech giants like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google.

Mega-IPOs follow a familiar script: limited initial float and heavy oversubscription engineer an immediate scarcity pop, followed almost inevitably by a post-IPO correction once reality catches up to hype, and the more the initial valuation of a company is detached from the underlying financial reality the more severe the correction will be. 

Knowing that dynamic, I concluded this IPO could only be played profitably by securing an allocation at the offer price and flipping it immediately as live trading began, cashing in on the predictable day-one pop while passing the valuation risk on to the institutional and retail FOMO buyers still chasing the AI narrative. Already everyone who bought shares today in the market is in the red.

To be clear, I am genuinely long-term bullish on AI. Just as businesses gradually figured out how to optimize the internet after the dot-com era to unlock massive productivity and profits, corporations will eventually master AI to transform their bottom lines. However, separating today’s market euphoria from underlying business fundamentals reveals why a $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation for a standalone frontier AI lab leaves virtually no margin of safety and no path to profitability.

⚫The CapEx Treadmill and the Enterprise ROI Lag

Unlike traditional enterprise software companies that build a core platform once and enjoy 80%+ gross margins for decades on recurring seats and maintenance, frontier AI labs are locked onto a permanent hardware replacement treadmill. AI data center infrastructure currently has an effective lifecycle of roughly 18 to 24 months. Every two years, compute providers must essentially replace their entire hardware fleets, and those colossal capital costs are passed straight down to labs like Anthropic, which already carries roughly $901 billion in long-term compute commitments alongside a $104 billion net loss over the first nine months of 2026 alone. 

That GAAP figure is dominated by non-cash fair-value adjustments, yet the operating picture does not reverse the conclusion: the single quarter of operating profit was followed by a swing back into loss, the nine-month operating result stayed negative, and the underlying pattern of high compute intensity plus locked-in multi-year commitments has not eased.

At the same time, pure-play labs lack real pricing power. Just like executives during the early dot-com years, most corporate CEOs today are still searching for ways to generate clear, measurable financial ROI from AI deployments. Because current models are not yet fully mature (still prone to hallucinations, subtle logic flaws, or unintended autonomous agent behavior), enterprises remain cautious to cut the workforce as intense human supervision is still needed. 
And Anthropic’s core audience is businesses, making this corporate deployment lag hit its revenue model directly. Anthropic’s heavier enterprise weighting (versus a larger consumer layer) makes the test more direct, because most of its revenue sits in the segment where the ROI lag, switching ease, and incomplete workflow embedding are most visible. 

And because AI still sits in a relatively thin application layer for most use cases today, companies can easily switch models from month to month if another one looks better in the leading benchmarks, preventing Anthropic from simply raising prices to cover its escalating compute bills. The commercial transition remains incomplete: most enterprises have not yet embedded AI deeply into core workflows the way SAP or Microsoft products are embedded. That is the specific gap that must be closed before durable pricing power and switching costs can appear.

⚫The Resource Allocation Catch-22

To build true pricing power, stability, and durable margins, Anthropic must help businesses monetize AI while embedding itself so deeply into core corporate processes that switching becomes practically unthinkable, the way Microsoft or SAP are woven into a company’s daily financial, operational, and governance backbone.

Here lies the fatal operational Catch-22 for a standalone lab: making that transition requires diverting billions of dollars and top engineering talent away from pure model scaling and toward building specialized corporate ecosystems. Yet the frontier model race moves so relentlessly fast that skipping even a single development cycle risks dropping from a market leader to a middle-tier or lagging player, instantly eroding API revenue and relevance. Pure-play labs simply do not have the spare cash or engineering bandwidth to fight both battles at the same time. Independent survival requires free cash flow generation large and durable enough to finance the commercial embedding and specialized-product track and the continuous frontier model race simultaneously. Pure-plays lack the other high-margin businesses that let the major platforms absorb that dual load.

⚫The Two-Tier AI Future and Geopolitical Lock-In

Over time, the AI landscape will naturally fracture into two distinct tiers with very different economics:

◾The Commercial Tier: Everyday enterprise AI will increasingly commoditize into specialized, lower-CapEx models deeply embedded inside corporate workflows. Once a lab successfully transitions here, switching costs rise, hardware intensity moderates, and more reliable pricing power can finally emerge.

◾The Frontier Tier: For defense, intelligence, and elite cutting-edge tech sectors, the R&D race will never slow down. Major world powers are locked into a strategic arms race where allowing a rival to gain even a temporary decisive edge could destabilize deterrence or erode second-strike capability. For both offense and defense, staying at the absolute frontier is non-negotiable regardless of cost. so that keeps the ai companies locked in that same race.

⚫Phase 1 Burn to Phase 2 Tech-Titan Consolidation

Standalone labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are caught right in the middle of this squeeze and lack the balance sheets to survive it indefinitely. Once Phase 1 capital fatigue sets in and both retail and institutional investors grow tired of funding endless cash burn, stock valuations will inevitably compress.

That sets the stage for Phase 2 consolidation. 
Diversified, cash-rich tech titans like Google (already backing Gemini), Amazon, Microsoft, alongside ecosystems like SpaceX/xAI, possess massive, profitable core product lines that can subsidize permanent frontier R&D while simultaneously building out deeply embedded enterprise ecosystems. Amazon and Google’s large stakes in Anthropic function as strategic prepositioning as they see that next phase already clearly, and as a call option on that future consolidation. Their stakes do not serve as an operating subsidy that already solves pure-play economics or supplies the diversified cash flows needed to fund both tracks. While consolidation of top AI labs into a handful of tech giants will raise eyebrows among regulators, Washington will almost certainly override antitrust objections on national security, defense, and intelligence grounds to preserve U.S. AI leadership, leaving top frontier labs under the direct or de facto control of established tech giants.

⚫The Long-Term Takeaway

AI is real, and over the coming decade companies will unlock enormous profits from it, just as they did once the dot-com dust settled. Until that transition happens and valuations reflect the true capital intensity of the business, hype-driven IPO pops are opportunities to lock in disciplined gains, not to hold through the inevitable shakeout.

Disclaimer; this is not financial advice but simply my analysis as a retail investor after looking into Anthropic's Quarterly reports, their prospectus and the wider AI market. I hope you find it useful but apply critical thinking to what anyone says, including what i wrote.
